facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Both the destruction of the Darkholds and Scarlet Witch's death from Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness are referenced.
The series was originally Agatha: House of Harkness until it was changed to Agatha: Coven of Chaos on July 23, 2022.
The working title was "My Pretty".
The series changed its name again from Agatha: Coven of Chaos to Agatha: Darkhold Diaries on September 1, 2023.
It was changed again from Agatha: Darkhold Diaries to Agatha on March 11, 2024.
It was changed once again from Agatha to Agatha: The Lying Witch With Great Wardrobe on May 13, 2024.
It was finally changed to Agatha All Along on May 14, 2024.
This is the first Marvel Studios series to feature a formal showrunner; previous series were created by head writers and had production overseen by Marvel Studios executives.

During the production, Sasheer Zamata suggested to the the creator of the show to include the history of the imagery of broomsticks and witches. While she had Kathryn Hahn's support on the suggestion, Jac Schaeffer politely turned it down noting that "it’s still a Disney show. It’s still on Disney+".
This is the Marvel Studios product that has been renamed the most, being renamed five times.
The final logo for Agatha All Along has a Marvel Television logo above it, unlike the previous five logos which all sported the Marvel Studios logo.

Every episode title of Agatha All Along is a lyric from the Ballad of the Witches' Road. While most of the episodes' titles come from the Sacred Chant version, the title of the fourth episode comes from Lorna Wu's version.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Many characters from the movies and one-shots have appeared in recurring or guest roles, such as Peggy Carter, Howard Stark, Anton Vanko, Dum Dum Dugan and Arnim Zola.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Stan Lee, one of the main Marvel Comics writers and one of the co-creators of the character Peggy Carter in Marvel Comics, has appeared in a small part in the series after having appeared in many Marvel productions before.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: References to the events of the only film chronologically set before the series, Captain America: The First Avenger are made through the show, naming major characters Captain America, Red Skull and Abraham Erskine.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The opening of the first episode, Now is Not the End, used archive footage of Peggy Carter from Captain America: The First Avenger and Marvel One-Shot: Agent Carter during a montage sequence.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The journalist B. Hornbuckle of The New York Examiner, who wrote an article shown in Captain America: The First Avenger, also reported on Howard Stark's trials by the United States Congress.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Peggy Carter's first attire in the episode Now is Not the End consist of red, white and blue clothes, as a tribute to Captain America's Uniform.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: After its introduction in the first Captain America film, the Strategic Scientific Reserve plays an important role in the series.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In Now is Not the End, Captain America's USO Show is mentioned.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the first episode of the series, the Stark Expo is featured.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Howard Stark's work with Vita Radiation during Project Rebirth, as seen in Captain America: The First Avenger, are the basis for his development of Molecular Nitramene.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Roxxon Corporation is prominently featured for the first time after having been teased in Iron Man, Iron Man 2, Iron Man 3, the Marvel One-Shot: A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Thor's Hammer and Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.. Roxxon would later play significant roles in other MCU TV series like Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., Daredevil, Cloak & Dagger and Helstrom.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Before appearing in a live-action production set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Edwin Jarvis had been already referenced through J.A.R.V.I.S., an AI constructed by Tony Stark honoring the actual Jarvis. Jarvis also had an appearance in the comic Iron Man 2: Public Identity. Jarvis even makes a meta-reference to the J.A.R.V.I.S. AI, stating that he has no desire to spend the rest of his time as a disembodied voice.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Howard Stark's behavior mirrors Tony Stark's, such as being considered a millionaire playboy, or mocking the United States Congress when facing a committee.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The concept of Howard Stark having a vault in his basement for the inventions he did not want to fall in the wrong hands is very similar to the armor vault that his son Tony Stark would have in the basement of his own mansion to keep his Iron Man Armors.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Peggy Carter's excuse for refusing a dance with a man in the episode Now is Not the End, being afraid to step in his toes, is very similar to the last phrase that Steve Rogers told her before crashing into the Arctic and losing the connection.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The song Star Spangled Man can be heard throughout the episode Bridge and Tunnel.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Captain America Adventure Program is introduced in the MCU.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Peggy Carter tells Hugh Jones that her first name is "Agent", when he mistook her for a secretary. This is a recurring joke in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, when Tony Stark assured that Phil Coulson's first name was "Agent" in The Avengers, before acknowledging him as "Phil" following his death. This joke occurs again in the episode Better Angels, in a conversation between Carter and Whitney Frost.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Peggy Carter's quote "I'd been wallowing in it since the war, wondering why no one would give Agent Peggy Carter a shot." is a meta-fictional reference to her own Marvel One-Shot.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Before making a proper appearance in the series, Ana Jarvis' voice can be heard in the episode Time and Tide.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the fourth episode of Season One the device Blitzkrieg Button is revealed to have one vial from Steve Rogers's blood. The origin of this vial is first seen in Captain America: The First Avenger where Rogers has twelve vials being filled with samples of his blood in a further attempt to recreate the Super Soldier Serum.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The New York Bulletin is introduced in the MCU.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The alcoholic drink brand "O'Harren's Scotch Whisky" is introduced.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Agent Carter is Marvel Television's first female led property.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Red Room is introduced and depicts the beginnings of the Black Widow Program, which would be the training place of Black Widow.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The 107th Infantry Regiment and Howling Commandos are depicted in the episode The Iron Ceiling.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The scene with Peggy Carter carrying Captain America's Shield in Valediction would later have his pay-off in the Marvel Studios' animated TV series What If...? which depicts an alternate version of Carter as Captain Carter.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the season one finale, the way Peggy Carter talks to Howard Stark on the radio as he is flying a plane mirrors the way she talked to Steve Rogers, but this time she managed to save the person she was trying to save.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Howard Stark mentioning Rogers as his greatest creation further connects with the film Captain America: Civil War where Howard's son has a major conflict with Rogers.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Arnim Zola's cameo at the season one finale tie-ins with the storyline of Hydra infiltrating within S.H.I.E.L.D.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: As a meta-reference to the whole concept of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Peggy Carter states that she does not believe that movies based on comic books can be successful.

Some of the characters from Marvel Comics adapted into the show during its first season are Edwin Jarvis, Roger Dooley, Leet Brannis, Hugh Jones, Jerome Zandow, Ernst Mueller, Happy Sam Sawyer, Junior Juniper, Pinky Pinkerton and Johann Fennhoff. In the second season the number increases with Whitney Frost, Jason Wilkes, Calvin Chadwick, Thomas Gloucester and Joseph Manfredi.

The character of Elizabeth "Betsy" Ross, a Golden Age character that heavily influenced the character of Peggy Carter in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, is referenced with Carter's middle name being Elizabeth, and her fictional counterpart in The Captain America Adventure Program, Betty Carver.

Leviathan, the criminal organization responsible for the theft of Howard Stark's technology, is a mysterious organization in the comics that was created in the Communist Bloc just like Hydra was created in the Third Reich.
Peggy Carter is nicknamed Miss Union Jack. Union Jack is the alias of James Montgomery Falsworth in the comics.
The Council of Nine is the counterpart of the Secret Empire.

One of Angie Martinelli's neighbours works for Goodman, Kurtzberg & Holliway, a law firm derived from the comics, whose full name is Goodman, Lieber, Kurtzberg & Holliway, and named for Marvel founders Martin Goodman, Stan Lee (born Stanley Lieber) and Jack Kirby (born Jacob Kurtzberg).

The movies where Whitney Frost has starred are references to different mythos in the comics, especially regarding the comics version of the character: "The "F" Stands for Freedom" is a reference to a famous line uttered by the Ultimate Marvel version of Captain America: "Do you think this letter on my head stands for France?"; "The Woman with the Golden Face" is a reference to Madame Masque's signature mask in the comics; "Tales of Suspense" is a reference to the comic book series where both Madame Masque and Jason Wilkes first appeared; "The Nefarious Daughter" is a reference to Whitney Frost's birth name, Giuletta Nefaria, and being the daughter of Count Nefaria.
Anvil Studios, the motion picture company were Whitney Frost worked, is an horror pictures studios from the comics, where the actor Martin Preston previously worked.
The title of episode 1.01, Now is Not the End, is a reference to Peggy Carter's on-going adventures despite the loss of Steve Rogers, and how she moves on with her life thinking Rogers has died.
The title of episode 1.02, Bridge and Tunnel, is a reference to the bridges and tunnels that connect New York City to the mainland, and more specifically, New Jersey.
The title of episode 1.03, Time and Tide, is a reference to the quote "Time and tide wait for no man".

The title of episode 1.04, The Blitzkrieg Button, is the name of a device that allegedly would cut out the electric grids in a considerable area. The term Blitzkrieg is a method of warfare used by the German armed forces during World War II.
The title of episode 1.05, The Iron Ceiling, is a portmanteau of the terms Iron Curtain and Glass ceiling.
The title of episode 1.06, A Sin to Err, is a reference to an old Soviet cipher phrase.
The title of episode 1.07, SNAFU, is a military slang acronym meaning "Situation Normal: All Fucked Up."

The title of episode 1.08, Valediction, is defined as an expression to say farewell, which Carter did with her emotional attachment to Steve Rogers, after she asked Howard Stark to do the same. Also, this was the season finale before a second season was approved.
The title of episode 2.01, The Lady in the Lake, describing Jane Scott, is a reference to the Raymond Chandler's 1943 detective novel The Lady in the Lake.
The title of episode 2.02, A View in the Dark, is a twist of the saying "a shot in the dark".
The title of episode 2.03, Better Angels, is a reference to Abrahan Lincoln's first inaugural address, where he called the "better angels of our nature" to avoid conflict.
The title of episode 2.04, Smoke & Mirrors, is a reference to the common metaphor smoke and mirrors in where after examination, something appears to be an illusion.
The title of episode 2.05, The Atomic Job, is a reference to the movie The Italian Job.
The title of episode 2.06, Life of the Party, is a reference to the saying "the life of the party".

The title of episode 2.07, Monsters, is a reference to Whitney Frost's quote to dissuade Joseph Manfredi from shooting Ana Jarvis, saying that they were not monsters, only to end up shooting Ana Jarvis herself.
The title of episode 2.08, The Edge of Mystery, is a reference to a quote from J. Robert Oppenheimer.
The title of episode 2.09, A Little Song and Dance, is both a reference to the saying "song and dance" and the episode itself as it starts with a musical number.
The title of episode 2.10, Hollywood Ending, is a reference to the saying "hollywood ending".

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Many characters from the movies and one-shots have appeared in recurring or guest roles, such as Phil Coulson, Maria Hill, Nick Fury, Tyler, Felix Blake, Jasper Sitwell, Sif, Peggy Carter, Dum Dum Dugan, Jim Morita, List, Matthew Ellis, Gideon Malick and Wolfgang von Strucker.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: References to previous films in the franchise, especially The Avengers are made through the show, naming the Avengers as a team as well as individual members Iron Man, Captain America, Thor, Hulk, Hawkeye, and Black Widow.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The episode Pilot uses archive footage from Iron Man, The Incredible Hulk, Iron Man 2, Thor, and The Avengers.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The Centipede Device is said to be a mix of all previous known sources of super-powers, mixing the Super Soldier Serum (that gave Captain America his powers), gamma radiation (that gave Hulk his powers), and Extremis (that gave Aldrich Killian and other A.I.M. members their powers), all in blood injector made from Chitauri metal.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: In the Pilot, Maria Hill says that "Agent Coulson has requisitioned a Mobile Command Unit". Mobile Command Unit has the same initials as the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Stark Industries logo can be seen on the side of a bus at the beginning of Pilot.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: At the end of Pilot, Coulson says that they have yet to "cut the head off the Centipede", which references the motto of Hydra: "Cut off one head, two more will take its place."

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: WHiH World News is featured in the series, after having previously appeared in The Incredible Hulk, Iron Man 2, The Avengers Prelude: Fury's Big Week, Iron Man 2 Adaptation, and The Avengers.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: It is revealed that Thor's hammer Mjølnir was labeled as an 0-8-4 by S.H.I.E.L.D. when it first appeared in New Mexico.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The Pick-Lock Device used by Phil Coulson in Girl in the Flower Dress is a reference to the Iron Man film, as Coulson uses the device in exactly the same way: He asks for the device to one of his subordinates just raising his hand, and after pressing the button, he waits for the explosion with his arms folded across his chest.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The walls in the interrogation room in the Bus are built from a silicon-carbide Vibranium alloy. Vibranium is the same material used to create Captain America's Shield. This material is also used in the Toolbox.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Hydra and A.I.M. are referred as evil organizations comprised of brilliant scientists.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Emil Blonsky's fate after the events depicted in The Incredible Hulk is revealed. He is contained in a cryo-cell in Barrow, Alaska.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The gas station depicted in Repairs belongs to the Roxxon Corporation, previously referred to in the Iron Man, Iron Man 2, Iron Man 3, and Marvel One-Shot: A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Thor's Hammer. Roxxon was also subsequently portrayed in Agent Carter, Daredevil, Cloak & Dagger, Helstrom and Wonder Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Phil Coulson's "Cellist" former girlfriend from The Avengers is referenced both by Coulson and Raina before being formally introduced, revealing her name as Audrey Nathan.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Audrey Nathan says that Phil Coulson was "like out of a movie". This is a reference to Coulson's first appearances in the films Iron Man, Iron Man 2, Thor and The Avengers before appearing in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The Destroyer Armor Prototype Gun that Phil Coulson used to defeat the Centipede Soldiers in Beginning of the End is the same he used to challenge Loki in The Avengers. He even paraphrases himself stating "I know what it does". The weapon is also used by Agent Leo Fitz in Who You Really Are.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The first season directly crossover with Captain America: The Winter Soldier, with the Hydra Uprising being a plot on the show, while the second season includes connections to Avengers: Age of Ultron.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Culver University appears in the series, after having previously appeared in The Incredible Hulk and mentioned in Thor.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The show introduces the Kree to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The alien race is featured later in Guardians of the Galaxy and Captain Marvel.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Damage Control is mentioned in the episode Watchdogs, having previously been mentioned in Iron Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The episode Emancipation is set in the aftermath of the Battle at Leipzig-Halle Airport from Captain America: Civil War, with a WHiH News report on Steve Rogers and Tony Stark. The show also deals with the Sokovia Accords.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: With the book of spells known as the Darkhold, the fourth season ties-in with the mystical and supernatural concepts introduced in Doctor Strange.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The episodes Option Two, The One Who Will Save Us All, The Force of Gravity, and The End all mention the events of Avengers: Infinity War, with The One Who Will Save Us All revealing that the Confederacy wished to exploit Earth of it's resources before Thanos, who was name dropped in the episode, could attack.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The episode What We're Fighting For revealed that S.H.I.E.L.D. had Time-Travelled to an alternate timeline using the Quantum Realm, which was a source of time travel in the film Avengers: Endgame, and featured in the films Ant-Man, Ant-Man and the Wasp, and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. introduces the Darkforce in the episode The Only Light in the Darkness. The element was a plot thread on the second season of Agent Carter.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: Michael Carter, Stewart Carter, and Amanda Carter are listed as Peggy's family members in the obituary that Coulson reads in Emancipation.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: Isodyne Energy from Agent Carter is mentioned in the episode The Good Samaritan. It is revealed that all their assets were acquired by the Roxxon Corporation. This would go on to connect to both Cloak & Dagger and Wonder Man, with Isodyne's investigations into the Dark Dimension being continued by Roxxon in the two shows.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: The fictional drink brand "O'Harren's Scotch Whisky" that appeared previously in Agent Carter, as well as Daredevil, The Punisher, and Cloak & Dagger, appears in the episode Many Heads, One Tale. It makes a second appearance in The New Deal.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: Daniel Sousa (and his alternate version) is featured in the final season of Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., while direct references are made to organizations, locations, and other characters of Agent Carter. Hugh Jones, Isodyne Energy, the Council of Nine, and Auerbach Theatrical Agency are mentioned in the episode Alien Commies from the Future!; Edwin Jarvis, Ana Jarvis, and Howard Stark's Estate are mentioned in the book A History of S.H.I.E.L.D., as shown in the episode Out of the Past. Archive footage from Agent Carter episodes is also used in the episode; Roger Dooley is mentioned in the episode A Trout in the Milk.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / The Defenders Saga
facts.text: WZTM News appears in the episode Watchdogs, reporting on the Attack on the ATCU Storage Facility from S.H.I.E.L.D. Additionally, a news ticker says: "GANG WAR RAGES IN HELL'S KITCHEN. AUTHORITIES SEARCHING FOR SOLUTION". This is a reference to the ongoing conflicts between different criminal factions featured in Daredevil.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / The Defenders Saga
facts.text: New York Bulletin appears in the episode Ascension. The newspaper from New York City published an article titled "Quake: Hero or Rogue?".

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / The Defenders Saga
facts.text: In The Patriot, Yuri Zaikin fires a Judas Bullet at Mace during a press conference.

Some of the characters from Marvel Comics adapted into the show during its first season are Mike Peterson, Franklin Hall, Victoria Hand, Donnie Gill, John Garrett, Lorelei, Glenn Talbot, Eric Koenig and Marcus Daniels. In the second season, the number increases with Lance Hunter, Daniel Whitehall, Alphonso Mackenzie, Isabelle Hartley, Carl Creel, Calvin Zabo, Agent 33, Bobbi Morse and Marcus Scarlotti. For the third season, the number of characters increases again with Lash, Werner von Strucker, Hive, Elena Rodriguez, Hellfire, Holden Radcliffe and Aida. For the fourth season, the number of characters increases again with Robbie Reyes, Gabe Reyes, Jeffrey Mace, Canelo, Eli Morrow and Johnny Blaze. For the fifth season the number of characters increases with the debut of Flint, Maston-Dar and Rick Stoner.
The series marks the debut of various aliens species in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including the Kree, Vrellnexians, Kallusians, Astrans, and Rajaks.

Due to their popularity, the original characters from the show were adapted to the regular Marvel Comics Universe continuity in a new S.H.I.E.L.D. series, adapting Melinda May, Jemma Simmons and Leo Fitz, along with the previously introduced Phil Coulson. Grant Ward appeared in the second series based on the TV series, Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
Although Chan Ho Yin is an original character, the codename "Scorch" has been frequently used in the comics by characters with powers similar to Chan's.

Raina shares her name with a character from the comic books, a member of the Hauk'ka from the Savage Land. Though she does not appear to be based on this character, a reference to her having the same name is made in Beginning of the End when John Garrett tells Raina that they are "prehistoric creatures." Later, a character based on Ruth Negga's appearance and portrayal of Raina was introduced in the mainstream comics as an Inhuman.

The series uses the term "Gifted," the title of one of the story arcs from Joss Whedon's run on Astonishing X-Men, to refer to people with powers, presumably due to the fact that 20th Century Fox owns the rights to the X-Men, and even the mutant concept.
The Bus' official designation as "S.H.I.E.L.D. 6-1-6" is a reference to the main Marvel Comics continuity, called Earth-616.

In Yes Men, Sif mentions many alien races that are acknowledged to exist before their first formal appearance in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, such as Interdites, Pheragots, Levians, Sarks, Centaurians and the Kree.
Skye references the well known "With great power comes great responsibility" Ben Parker's quote in Pilot, although she changes the ending before finishing the quote.
During their first mission, Jemma Simmons describes their future missions as a "Journey into Mystery", referencing a long-running Marvel series, where Thor made his first appearance.
The truck emblazoned "Rocky Mountain Office Supplies" in The Asset is a reference to the complex in the Rocky Mountains where Graviton was created in the comics.
Leo Fitz's recurring references to Professor Vaughn are most likely references to Wendell Vaughn.
Some of the writing in the chalkboard inside the Todorov Building in Eye-Spy is written using the Skrull alphabet from the comics.

Skye refers to Phil Coulson behavior in The Hub as a "robot version of himself". This is a reference to the Life-Model Decoys, androids capable of recreating the likeness of a human, that was also referenced by Tony Stark in The Avengers. The Life-Model Decoys were later introduced in the fourth season.
Both H.A.M.M.E.R. and A.R.M.O.R. are listed as having their own sectors of The Hub in its floor map.
The Overkill Device first appeared in the comics as the Overkill Horn.

After the Battle of Greenwich, Skye wondered which other deities could be aliens, explicitly citing Vishnu. Vishnu and other Hindu Gods are characters in Marvel Comics belonging to a race called the Daevas from a world called Nirvana. This reference has caused criticism from real-life Hindus.
Leo Fitz references the catchphrase "Embrace the Change" in The Magical Place, used to promote the Secret Invasion event in the comics.
Skye being called "Doctor Nugent" by Jemma Simmons when she phoned after being expelled from the team in The Magical Place is most likely a reference to Alice Nugent.
Most items from the Howling Commando Gear are based on items that appeared in S.H.I.E.L.D. comics during the 1960s.

The main antagonists from the first two seasons, John Garrett and Daniel Whitehall, were members of the Great Wheel of the Zodiac, a collection of eleven of the most experienced espionage leaders in the world gathered by its twelfth member, Leonardo Da Vinci. Other prominent members that already appeared in the Marvel Cinematic Universe were Nick Fury, Dum Dum Dugan and Baron Strucker, and all of them have appeared or been prominently mentioned in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
Bobbi Morse's hair is black during her work undercover on Hydra. This is a reference one of her first appearance in the comics.

When the fourth season debuted the character of Robbie Reyes, it added several references to past versions of the Ghost Rider. In Lockup, there is a poster for Quentin Carnival, an old stunt bike, a black leather jacket and a chain inside of the abandoned basement where the Darkhold. All of these are nods to the character of Johnny Blaze who later appears in the episode The Good Samaritan in a flashback.

In the fifth season, Elena Rodriguez jokes about the existence of the comic book organization S.W.O.R.D., by asking if S.H.I.E.L.D. had a subdivision that was in charge of space travel and defense against alien attacks called S.P.E.A.R. This also references an organization from the Marvel Comics, though this one is a Chinese intelligence agency.
In the episode All the Comforts of Home, Ruby Hale's room has a poster of the Marvel Comics band, Steeltown Rockers.

Season 5 also changes the way Elena Rodriguez loses her arms, like in the Secret Warriors comic book series, from where she originates. Instead of Tomi Shishido, a member of Hydra and the Hand, it is Ruby Hale who cuts her limbs.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Melinda May's Phone Box
facts.text: Many of the phone contacts on Melinda May's phone are a reference to comic book characters or different individuals: "J.Larner" is a reference to James Larner, an agent of the MI; "Agent 60" in the comics is Kuro Chin, a Japanese double-agent working for S.H.I.E.L.D; "Nat" is a reference to Natasha Romanoff; "Lt. Stone" is a reference to Lieutenant Marcus Stone, an officer of the New York City Police Department; "M.Huff" is a reference to Margaret Huff, a S.H.I.E.L.D. agent and Nick Fury's former secretary in the comics; "Bell" is a reference to Jeffrey Bell, executive producer of Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D; "Woo" is a reference to Jimmy Woo; "Lt.Crouch" is a reference to Joe Crouch, a member of the series' art department.
Each of the D.W.A.R.F.s used by Leo Fitz and Jemma Simmons are named after one of the Seven Dwarfs from the 1937 Disney film, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.
Mack's name and role as a trucker is an homage to the character Mack, an animated truck in the Disney-Pixar film Cars.
The quote about a "magic broom" to clean up the damages made by the battle between Thor and Malekith is a reference to the famous segment The Sorcerer's Apprentice from the movie Fantasia.
In A Fractured House, Bobbi Morse can be seen wearing a Star Wars shirt.
In Ascension, while Phil Coulson is using a hologram to stall Hive, he mimics Princess Leia's message to Obi-Wan Kenobi from Star Wars: A New Hope.
In The Good Samaritan, Phil Coulson and Jeffrey Mace argue about Han Solo and Admiral Ackbar being heroes, as well as mentioning the Rebels and the Empire.

facts.section: References to Joss Whedon's Previous Works
facts.text: Many actors that have appeared in recurring or special guest roles have previously worked as cast members of Joss Whedon's previous TV series and films. J. August Richards previously portrayed Charles Gunn in the series Angel; Ron Glass previously portrayed Shepherd Book in the series Firefly and the movie Serenity; Tzi Ma previously portrayed Matsu in the series Dollhouse; Elsi Eng previously portrayed a member of the additional cast in Much Ado About Nothing; Vincent Laresca previously portrayed Mr. Sunshine in the series Dollhouse; Ilia Volok previously portrayed Marco in the series Firefly; Christopher Gehrman previously portrayed Rudy in the series Angel; Patton Oswalt previously portrayed Joel Mynor in the series Dollhouse; Amy Acker previously portrayed Winifred Burkle in the series Angel and Beatrice in the film Much Ado About Nothing; Glenn Morshower previously portrayed Mr. Newton in the series Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Sheriff Rand in the series Dollhouse; Reed Diamond previously portrayed Laurence Dominic in the series Dollhouse and Don Pedro in the film Much Ado About Nothing; Denney Pierce previously portrayed Vic in the series Angel; Jarrod Crawford previously portrayed Rondell in the series Angel; Chase Kim previously portrayed Male Active in the series Dollhouse; Brian Tee previously portrayed Intern in the series Buffy the Vampire Slayer; facts.section: References to Joss Whedon's Previous Works
facts.text: The weapon first used by Grant Ward in 0-8-4 first appeared in the movie Serenity, written and directed by Joss Whedon.

facts.section: References to Joss Whedon's Previous Works
facts.text: The final scene from The Well references Joss Whedon's series Dollhouse. The question "Did I fall asleep?" that Phil Coulson asks, and the answer "For a little while." by his masseuse, are a direct quote from Dollhouse, where this is said to the actives every time they are wiped.
The title of episode 1.01, Pilot, is the standard title of the first episode of a series.
The title of episode 1.02, 0-8-4, is a reference to the central artifact of the episode and also the code used to designate artifacts of unknown origin.
The title of episode 1.03, The Asset, is a reference to the code used to designate some of S.H.I.E.L.D.'s the most prominent scientist, including Franklin Hall.
The title of episode 1.04, Eye-Spy, is a play in the title of the television series I Spy.

The title of episode 1.05, Girl in the Flower Dress, was chosen after Ruth Negga's character Raina. During production, the title of the episode was going to be Scorch, but by the time it was shot, Negga's performance impressed so much the producers that they renamed the episode to reference her character.
The title of episode 1.06, FZZT, is one of the possible onomatopoeias for an electric shock.
The title of episode 1.07, The Hub, is the name of one of S.H.I.E.L.D.'s most important facilities.
The title of episode 1.08, The Well, is a reference to one of Grant Ward's episodes of child abuse by his family, where he was forced to throw his younger brother into a well by his older brother.
The title of episode 1.09, Repairs,.
The title of episode 1.10, The Bridge, is a reference to the location at the end of the episode where Phil Coulson was kidnapped.
The title of episode 1.11, The Magical Place, is a reference to Phil Coulson's reaction to Tahiti.
The title of episode 1.12, Seeds,.
The title of episode 1.13, T.R.A.C.K.S., refers to the major set piece of the episode, where Coulson's team heist goes awry.
The title of episode 1.14, T.A.H.I.T.I., refers to the Project T.A.H.I.T.I. that saved Phil Coulson's life.
The title of episode 1.15, Yes Men, is a reference to Lorelei's powers of enthralling men.
The title of episode 1.16, End of the Beginning, refers to the conclusion of the first arc of Season One.

The title of episode 1.17, Turn, Turn, Turn, is a direct quotation by John Garrett in the previous episode, stating that everything is connected. The episode reveals the show's connection to the plot of Captain America: The Winter Soldier, with Garrett being a pivotal character in the plot.
The title of episode 1.18, Providence, refers to the secret facility manned by Eric Koenig named Providence.
The title of episode 1.19, The Only Light in the Darkness, refers to the description Blackout gave to Audrey Nathan when he professed his feeling for her.

The title of episode 1.20, Nothing Personal, is used twice in the episode to describe the separation of a professional agenda from intimate feelings, once by Grant Ward to Skye, then again by Deathlok to Ward.
The title of episode 1.21, Ragtag,.

The title of episode 1.22, Beginning of the End, was used John Garrett during his conversation with the United States Armed Forces. Episode 1.16 End of the Beginning and Episode 1.22 Beginning of the End are named as opposite of each other, and also serve to indicate that episode 1.16 through 1.22 are the last arc of Season One.
The title of episode 2.01, Shadows, is a reference to Phil Coulson's speech about S.H.I.E.L.D. has to operate in the shadows now.
The title of episode 2.02, Heavy Is the Head,.

The title of episode 2.03, Making Friends and Influencing People, is a play on the 1936 book How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie, referring to the plight of Jemma Simmons ("making friends") and the Faustus method ("influencing people").
The title of episode 2.04, Face My Enemy, refers to influenced Agent 33 using a Hydra technology to copy Melinda May's face and pass of as her.
The title of episode 2.05, A Hen in the Wolf House, is a reference to the increasing danger Jemma Simmons, played by Elizabeth Henstridge, faces as a double-agent in Hydra.

The title of episode 2.06, A Fractured House, is a reference to SHIELDS efforts to get their SHIELD agents to safe houses. The title could also be seen as a metaphor for Lance Hunter and Bobbi Morse's relationship.
The title of episode 2.07, The Writing on the Wall, refers to urge of Phil Coulson to engrave the Words of Creation on the wall.

The title of episode 2.08, The Things We Bury, refers to the site of Christian Ward's torturing of Thomas Ward, a well which had been buried by the brothers' parents. It also refers to the burial of the temporarily deceased Jiaying, who had been vivisected by Daniel Whitehall for his own gains.
The title of episode 2.09,...Ye Who Enter Here, is a reference to the inscription on the gates of hell in Dante's Inferno, "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here".
The title of episode 2.10, What They Become, is a reference to what Raina had said to Skye before they turned into Inhumans.
The title of episode 2.11, Aftershocks, is a reference to Skye's Inhuman powers.
The title of episode 2.12, Who You Really Are, is the question Skye ask herself as her inhuman powers become harder to control.
The title of episode 2.13, One of Us, is a reference to the 1932 film, Freaks, where the troupe members chant "One of us! One of us! Gooble Gobble! Gooble Gobble!"
The title of episode 2.14, Love in the Time of Hydra, is a play on Gabriel Garcia Marquez's novel Love in the Time of Cholera.
The title of episode 2.15, One Door Closes,.
The title of episode 2.16, Afterlife, is a direct reference to the village Afterlife, the home created by Jiaying for Inhumans.

The title of episode 2.17, Melinda, was chosen after Melinda May, and is the only episode to be directly named after one of the show's characters, as her backstory behind her nickname the Cavalry is finally given.
The title of episode 2.18, The Frenemy of My Enemy.
The title of episode 2.19, The Dirty Half Dozen, is a reference to the World War II film The Dirty Dozen.
The title of episode 2.20, Scars, comes from the conversation between Jiaying and Robert Gonzales where he compares his battle wounds to her experiences, both imposed by Hydra.
The title of episode 2.21, S.O.S. Part One, refers to the abbreviation for "Save Our Ship", in this case, the Iliad.
The title of episode 2.22, S.O.S. Part Two, refers to the abbreviation for "Save Our Ship", in this case, the Iliad.
The title of episode 3.01, Laws of Nature refers to President Matthew Ellis's speech, in which he stated that the laws of nature have changed.
The title of episode 3.02, Purpose in the Machine.
The title of episode 3.03, A Wanted (Inhu)man, refers to Lincoln Campbell and his status as a fugitive, incorporating that he is also an Inhuman.
The title of episode 3.04, Devils You Know.
The title of episode 3.05, 4,722 Hours, is a reference to the exact amount of time that Jemma Simmons spent stranded on another planet.
The title of episode 3.06, Among Us Hide..., is a reference to the comic Fantastic Four #45, titled Among Us Hide... the Inhumans! which introduces the Inhuman Royal Family.
The title of episode 3.07, Chaos Theory,.
The title of episode 3.08, Many Heads, One Tale, refers to how the different leaders of Hydra knew the story of the origin of the organization.

The title of episode 3.09, Closure, is a reference to a recurring motif in Grant Ward's storyline, having sought closure for his own childhood abuse, for Kara Palamas' torture and brainwashing, and then for Palamas' death.

The title of episode 3.10, Maveth, is a transliteration of the Hebrew word מָוֶת, meaning death, or more accurately, death by punishment. It has been featured recurringly in the season to refer to both the Monolith and the secret society related to it.

The title of episode 3.11, Bouncing Back, is a reference to Elena Rodriguez's powers, who allows moving at superhuman speed for the same amount of time as one of her heartbeats, before she is bounced back to her original position.
The title of episode 3.12, The Inside Man, is a reference to Hydra's mole in the symposium on the Inhumans in Taiwan.
The title of episode 3.13, Parting Shot, refers to the "spy's goodbye" given to Bobbi Morse and Lance Hunter which were disavowed by S.H.I.E.L.D.
The title of episode 3.14, Watchdogs, refers to the terrorist organization known as the Watchdogs.
The title of episode 3.15, Spacetime, refers to the lecture given by Leo Fitz, who was attempting the physics of the fourth-dimension after Daisy Johnson received a vision of the future.

The title of episode 3.16, Paradise Lost, is a reference to the book Paradise Lost owned by Gideon Malick's father, in which he hid a white stone to be used to cheat during ceremonies to determine who would enter the Monolith.
The title of episode 3.17, The Team, is a reference to the first activation and mission of the Secret Warriors.
The title of episode 3.18, The Singularity, refers to Leo Fitz's and Jemma Simmons' relationship, which they compared to a black hole and singularity.

The title of episode 3.19, Failed Experiments, refers to the experiments enacted by the Kree Reapers in order to create the Inhumans, which were deemed as mistakes. Hive also would be dubbed a "failed experiment" by a Reaper who was trying to kill him.
The title of episode 3.20, Emancipation, refers to the liberation of Daisy Johnson from Hive, who had swayed her with his parasites.
The title of episode 3.21, Absolution, refers to what Hive said to Daisy Johnson in the previous episode.
The title of episode 3.22, Ascension, is reference to Jesus' sacrifice to save humanity. In the episode, Lincoln Campbell sacrificed himself to kill Hive and save the human race.
The title of episode 4.01, The Ghost, refers to Ghost Rider and Lucy Bauer.

The title of episode 4.02, Meet the New Boss, is a reference to the line from the song "Won't Get Fooled Again" by The Who, referring to Phil Coulson meets with the new Director of S.H.I.E.L.D., Jeffrey Mace.
The title of episode 4.03, Uprising, is a reference to the Watchdogs attempting to stage a world power outage to capture Inhumans.
The title of episode 4.04, Let Me Stand Next to Your Fire, is a line from The Jimi Hendrix Experience song titled "Fire."
The title of episode 4.05, Lockup, is a reference to the fact that the agents need to South Ridge Penitentiary to get answers.
The title of episode 4.06, The Good Samaritan, refers to what Gabe Reyes called Johnny Blaze when he came and rescued him and Robbie.
The title of episode 4.07, Deals With Our Devils,.
The title of episode 4.08, The Laws of Inferno Dynamics, is a play on the words referencing the Laws of Thermodynamics.
The title of episode 4.09, Broken Promises,.
The title of episode 4.10, The Patriot, is a reference to Jeffrey Mace's codename.
The title of episode 4.11, Wake Up,.
The title of episode 4.12, Hot Potato Soup, is a reference to Operation Hot Potato, the plan used to conceal the location of the Darkhold.
The title of episode 4.13, BOOM, is a reference to Tucker Shockley's ability to self-detonate.
The title of episode 4.14, The Man Behind the Shield,.
The title of episode 4.15, Self Control,.
The title of episode 4.16, What If..., is a reference to the Marvel Comics series of the same name, which explored alternative scenarios in existing comic stories.
The title of episode 4.17, Identity and Change,.
The title of episode 4.18, No Regrets,.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Triskelion, which first appeared in Captain America: The Winter Soldier, makes its first chronological appearance in the 1989 intro scene, while still under construction.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: After Scott Lang's escape from jail, he flies into a cable car and lands on a man's newspaper. The letters that he lands on read "Who's to Blame for Sokovia?" Referencing the events of Avengers: Age of Ultron while also foreshadowing the events of Captain America: Civil War, Hank Pym mentions Sokovia later in the film, when he protests about the propose of calling the Avengers, stating that they were "too busy dropping cities down from the sky".

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the last scene of the movie when Luis tells Scott Lang that Sam Wilson is looking for him, in one of the transitions the fine lady Luis mentions said that "We got everything nowadays, we got a guy who swings, a guy who can climb up the walls." This alone foreshadows Spider-Man appearing in Captain America: Civil War.

Originally the film was meant to focus on Hank Pym, the original Ant-Man. However, the filmmakers deemed Pym as having a too family-unfriendly history. For example, Pym developed several split personalities; one of whom abused his girlfriend Janet van Dyne. It was then decided to focus on Pym's successor Scott Lang, with Pym becoming a mentor and supporting character.

Darren Cross mentions in a scene that the rumors he had heard about the Ant-Man were just "tales to astonish". This is a reference to the Marvel comic book series entitled Tales to Astonish; Ant-Man was first introduced in issue number 35.
Ant-thony's designation number 247, is a reference to the comics Tales to Astonish Vol 1 #27 and Marvel Premiere Vol 1 #47, the first appearances of Hank Pym and Scott Lang respectively.
In the Pym Residence, there was a decorative small red chair. In the comics, the first object Pym ever shrunk was a chair.
The tune that Luis whistles during the Infiltration into Pym Technologies Headquarters is "It's a Small World", the theme song of one of the rides in Disneyland, composed by the Sherman Brothers.
When Scott Lang is working at Baskin-Robbins, his name tag says 'Jack' and he called a colleague "Darby". Those are the names of Paul Rudd's children.
Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Paul Rudd were front-runners being considered for the lead role of Scott Lang, The role eventually went for Rudd.

Nathan Fillion was in the running to play Hank Pym before it was decided the character would not appear in The Avengers and never auditioned. Fillion was later supposed to portray Wonder Man in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 as a cameo but was later cut and the role went to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II for the Wonder Man show. He also portrayed Cory Pitzner/T.D.K. in the DC Extended Universe production The Suicide Squad.
Adrien Brody had been interested in playing Scott Lang.

Jessica Chastain turned down the lead female role of Hope van Dyne due to scheduling conflicts. Chastain later portrayed Vuk in the 20th Century Studios production Dark Phoenix, as she was desperate to have a role in a comic-book movie.
Concept Art showed that Arnim Zola was set to appear with Toby Jones reprising the role but the appearance was scrapped.

Early in production Peyton Reed considered casting Rick Moranis for a cameo role in the film. Moranis famously portrayed Wayne Szalinski, a scientist who creates shrinking technology in Honey, I Shrunk The Kids and its subsequent sequels Honey, I Blew Up The Kid and Honey, I Shrunk Ourselves produced by Walt Disney Pictures. Moranis had semi-retired from on screen acting with the occasional voice role following Honey, I Shrunk Ourselves release and had he appeared it would have been his first since then, but Reed ultimately felt the film had too many strategically placed cameos and felt if they were going to bring him back it would be for a more substantial role.
Patrick Wilson was originally cast as William Cross/Crossfire in the film before leaving when Edgar Wright left the project.
The film was shot under the name "BigFoot".
The film was announced at the 2012 San Diego Comic-Con along with Guardians of the Galaxy.

This film is the first time John Slattery has portrayed Howard Stark since Iron Man 2. In the interim, Dominic Cooper played a younger version of Howard Stark in the film Captain America: The First Avenger and the television series Agent Carter.

The idea of a potential Ant-Man movie had been kicked around before Marvel had its own film studio. Once the Marvel Cinematic Universe was established, there were plans to include him in the Phase One films and have him be a member of the Avengers. Those plans fell through, and he was instead supposed to have a film in Phase Two. The movie was then pushed back to become the first part of Phase Three... until it was decided that this movie would actually be the finale of Phase Two, after Avengers: Age of Ultron, and that Captain America: Civil War would lead Phase Three. In short, its release date changed less than its classification did.
Adam McKay, Ruben Fleischer, Rawson Marshall Thurber, Nicholas Stoller, Michael Dowse and David Wain were considered to direct the film.

Director Peyton Reed has given details on the film's original beginning and ending: "It was a standalone sequence, where you really did not see it was Hank Pym. He was retrieving some microfilm from, originally Cuban general and then [due to timeline continuity] a Panamanian general. It was designed in early drafts to be almost like a Bond movie standalone scene in the beginning. It was going to show the powers. You never saw Ant-Man. It almost felt like an Invisible Man sequence, and it’s really, really cool."; "At the end of the movie he gets away and has these Cross particles, and there was a sequence where Ant-Man has an encounter with him. But then for a couple reasons, it felt like maybe we should leave those particles out there. In that original thing, he took Martin Donovan out and got the particles."

In the scene where Ant-Man and Yellowjacket are fighting in the latter's suitcase, the date on the phone reads "Friday, 8 October". The Ant-Man film takes place in 2015, thus making this date incorrect, as the 8th was a Thursday in 2015.
The post-credits caption promises "Ant-Man will return".
On April 14, 2023, an ASL version of Ant-Man was added to Disney+, making Ant-Man the first, and as of 2026, the only, MCU film to have an ASL version.
Characters from the comics adapted for the movie are Jimmy Woo, Ghost, Sonny Burch, Bill Foster, and Elihas Starr.

Throughout the film, Cassie Lang expresses her wish to be a superhero like her father. In the comics, she indeed becomes a superhero with the names Stature and Stinger. She would eventually become a superhero in Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania.

As a recurring gag, Kurt Goreshter calls Ghost Baba Yaga, as he considers it similar to the Russian boogeyman. In the comics, Baba Yaga is a character commonly associated with both Captain Britain and X-Men's Colossus.

The return of Janet van Dyne from the Quantum Realm, known in the comics as the Microverse, also occurred during Avengers Vol #4 issues 32 to 34. Her look is also inspired by the outfit she sported during those issues in the Microverse, face mask and all.
Scott Lang is referred to as Giant-Man by the news outlet. This alias, though not usually used by Scott, is his official codename in the Ultimate Universe.
Scott being a part of a security company, is lifted from Nick Spencer's 2015 run of Ant-Man, where he hires former villains to be a part of it.

Ghost is male in the original comics and part of Iron Man's rogues gallery, never actually crossing paths with Ant-Man. His powers also come from his suit rather than the Quantum Realm. He eventually became an anti-hero after joining a team of superhumans called the Thunderbolts. Ghost would later appear in the Thunderbolts* film and is set to reappear in Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: This is the first time Janet van Dyne makes a fully-fledged appearance after her brief cameo in Ant-Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Bill Foster states that he worked with Hank Pym in Project G.O.L.I.A.T.H., which was mentioned in a deleted scene in Iron Man 2.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Jimmy Woo, whose existence was first hinted in the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. episode Face My Enemy, makes his first appearance in the MCU.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Scott Lang is in house arrest due to a deal with the government after the events of Captain America: Civil War. This status was first mentioned in Avengers: Infinity War.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Hank Pym and Hope van Dyne are fugitives due to the aftermath of the events of Captain America: Civil War.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: While talking with Hope, Sonny Burch says that both Hydra and S.H.I.E.L.D. are gone, as a result of the events depicted in the Marvel Cinematic Universe as a whole.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the post-credits scene, Hank, Hope, and Janet are killed due to Thanos' use of the Infinity Gauntlet in Infinity War.

This is the second MCU installment to have both male and female co-leads and have the names of the two characters in the title, the first being Cloak & Dagger. Coincidentally, both products were released in 2018. It is also the first movie to have a female character's name in the title.
The post-credits caption reads "Ant-Man and the Wasp will return?" (the first not to promise the further appearance of a character).
This is the first film to feature Ant-Man but not feature Falcon.
This is the first MCU product in which characters are killed on-screen due to the events of another product without being a flashback.
This is the second MCU film after Thor: Ragnarok to have a woman as the lead antagonist.
Paul Rudd learned some of the close up magic to prepare for the movie.
Langston Fishburne, Laurence Fishburne’s son, played the younger version of his character, Bill Foster.
For the role of Janet van Dyne, Evangeline Lilly had Michelle Pfeiffer on her wish list to play Janet, while Michael Douglas expressed the desire to have his wife Catherine Zeta-Jones play Janet.
Before production on the movie began, Evangeline Lilly requested for Hope to have a ponytail, stating that she "wants to sweat" while fighting to make her character more realistic.
The Ant-Man Suit and the Wasp Suit worn by Scott Lang and Hope van Dyne more accurately reflect the ones from the Marvel Comics.
Sub-Atomica is mentioned, in the comics, Subatomica is a solar system within the Microverse.
Krylar is a character from the comics who only appeared in one comic issue as a citizen of the planet Ky.
The city of Axia is similar to Kang the Conqueror's city of Chronopolis from the Marvel Comics.
This is the first appearance of Rama-Tut, Immortus, Mister Gryphon, and Victor Timely, all four Kang the Conqueror variants, as well as the Council of Kangs from the Marvel Comics.
The first appearance of the Council of Kangs matches 1988's Avengers #292 in which there is an auditorium full of Kangs.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Scott Lang and Jimmy Woo go out for lunch, a joke was made about them going to dinner in Ant-Man and the Wasp.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Scott Lang returns to Baskin-Robbins, his place of employment from the first Ant-Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Christine Everhart and WHiH Newsfront are mentioned as reviewers of Look Out for the Little Guy!, the first time WHiH Newsfront has been mentioned outside of WHiH Newsfront, a web series whose first season was promotion for the first Ant-Man film.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The events of the Blip from Avengers: Endgame are mentioned when Cassie Lang gets out of jail.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The events of the Time Heist, as well as Hulk and Rocket are mentioned in Scott Lang's book, Look Out for the Little Guy!.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The events of the Avengers Civil War from Captain America: Civil War are mentioned by Scott Lang.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Darren Cross returns after being presumed dead from the the first Ant-Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Thor and Mjølnir are mentioned by Victor Timely when he imprisoned Scott and Cassie Lang.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Incursions, a concept first introduced in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness is mentioned by Victor Timely.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The post-credits scene includes Loki and Mobius M. Mobius, and Victor Timely, setting up Loki season two.
This is Ruben Rabasa's second role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe after his role as Cardozo in the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. episode Who You Really Are.

This is David Dastmalchian's third role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe after his roles as Kurt Goreshter in Ant-Man and Ant-Man and the Wasp, and an alternate version of Kurt Goreshter in the What If...? episode What If... Zombies?!.
This is Katy M. O'Brian's second role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe after her role as Kimball in the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. episodes Brand New Day, The End is at Hand, and What We're Fighting For.
This is the 31st film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, which is also the same amount of ice cream flavors Baskin-Robbins has.
This is the first Marvel Studios opening introduction to include a villain, He Who Remains.
Scott Lang's book Look Out for the Little Guy! was produced as a real life book and is available for purchase.
A design easter egg to Rama-Tut was put in the Moon Knight episode The Friendly Type.
This is the first Ant Man film to not feature Michael Pena as Luis in any capacity.
This is the first MCU film where Loki appears without Thor himself.
Stan Lee recites his famous catchphrase "Excelsior!" for the first time in a film within the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Ultron is seen wearing a red cloak. In his first appearance (Avengers #54 1968), he wore one throughout the comic and had the alias of the Crimson Cowl.
When Vision rescues Wanda Maximoff and carries her away, they have a 'moment', referencing their relationship and eventual marriage in the comics.
The Mark XLV Iron Man used during the final battle is inspired by the Heroic Age armor.
This is the first live-action appearance of Tony Stark's Hulkbuster armor; it had previously appeared in various Marvel animated series and movies.
Scarlet Witch's costume from the end of the movie is inspired by her "Uncanny Avengers" uniform (a low-cut blouse and pants, with a coat on top).
In the comics, Ultron was an android with glowing eyes/mouth. One of Ultron's bodies in the film possesses these features as an homage to his comic appearance.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: All of the main, original Avengers in this film are manipulated in some way by Wanda Maximoff, with the exception of Hawkeye. Incidentally, Hawkeye was the only member of the original Avengers to be under the mind control of Loki in The Avengers.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The S.H.I.E.L.D. Helicarriers showing up at the final battle is part of S.H.I.E.L.D.'s protocol, Theta Protocol which was introduced in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

facts.section: References to Joss Whedon's Previous Works
facts.text: During Thor's vision, three men are seen wearing masks representing a wolf, a ram, and a hart (an archaic word for "stag"). In the TV series Angel, The Wolf, The Ram and The Hart were three ancient demons enacting their evil will on Earth as the senior partners of the law firm Wolfram & Hart, the primary antagonists of the series.

facts.section: Other Works that Reference Avengers: Age of Ultron
facts.text: In the episode Legends of Yesterday of the TV series Arrow, a part of a two-episode crossover with the other CW serial The Flash, Thea Queen comments on the assembling of a team in Laurel Lance's house in the countryside saying "A bunch of heroes in a farmhouse, feel like I've seen that before in a movie".

facts.section: Other Works that Reference Avengers: Age of Ultron
facts.text: In Marvel Pinball, there is a level themed around the Avengers: Age of Ultron. It was released as a part of the Cinematic alongside Avengers: Age of Ultron and Guardians of the Galaxy themed levels. These levels were re-released in the Marvel Pinball Cinematic Pack & Marvel Pinball collection in Pinball FX 2 and Pinball FX 3.
Mark Ruffalo revealed on Twitter that he worked with Andy Serkis on motion capture for the Hulk.
James Spader was Joss Whedon's first and only choice for the role of Ultron, because of his "hypnotic voice that can be eerily calm and compelling while also being very human and humorous".

The addition of Quicksilver to the cast sparked wide discussion over the direction of the character who is also slated to appear in X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014). Quicksilver had been discussed previously as a potential character in both X-Men: The Last Stand (2006) and The Avengers (2012), but legal complexities over the license to the character resulted in his omission from both films. However, in May 2013 both Marvel and Fox Studios announced a resolution to the previous legal issues, and that Quicksilver would appear in this film as well as an X-Men sequel, though under certain parameters: no allusion to his relations to the X-Men or Magneto (the character's father) could be made in an "Avengers" film, and no reference to Quicksilver's membership in the Avengers could be made in an "X-Men" film; the rights agreement between Fox and Marvel even goes so far as to stipulate the character cannot be referred to as a "mutant" in any Marvel film.

Scarlett Johansson was pregnant during filming of this movie so her scenes had to be fast-tracked before she began to show. For the action scenes, three stunt doubles were used and Johansson's face was digitally imposed with visual effects.
Saoirse Ronan was considered to play Wanda Maximoff.
This is the first film to feature War Machine without Pepper Potts and Happy Hogan.

Because Ultron was described as 8-9 feet tall, James Spader had to wear an antennae-like contraption made out of a thick piece of wire with two red balls attached to the top that went up his entire back and 3 feet above his head. This was done so that the actors that shared scenes with him would be able to have a reference point for where his eyes would be (the two red balls represented the placement of Ultron's eyes). Elizabeth Olsen stated that this was actually distracting because Spader would be giving an intense performance and out of instinct she would look at him rather than the balls representing his eyes. Much to everyone's amusement, whenever this happened, Aaron Taylor-Johnson would yell, "Red balls! Look at his balls, Lizzie!" at her in order to get her to look in the right direction.

Joss Whedon described this film as "smaller. More personal. More painful. The next thing that should happen to these characters, and not just a rehash of what worked the first time. A theme that is completely fresh and organic to itself."
In the first trailer, Ultron recites "No Strings On Me", a song from Pinocchio (1940), a Walt Disney film about an inanimate being who gains sentience; Ultron serves as a dark parallel of Pinocchio.

In the comics, Vision was created by Ultron to kill the Avengers. In this movie, he's created by Bruce Banner and Tony Stark, which also explains his color combination of Red, Green and Golden. Red and Golden are the combinations of Tony Stark's Iron Man armor and Green is the color of Hulk.
This is the second film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe that doesn't have a post credit scene.
This is the first Avengers film to be set in a 2.35:1 aspect ratio shot.

In Iron Man 3, if you look closely during the scene where Maya, Tony and Pepper are discussing the huge stuffed bunny in the living room, you can see Tony has hung a stocking for his A.I. J.A.R.V.I.S.. The stocking just so happens to be the same colors as Vision (red, green and yellow), the android that Tony and Bruce put JARVIS into in this film.
For the first time, a major hero (Quicksilver) dies permanently in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. All other Marvel heroes have either stayed alive, nearly died or been resurrected.

In the comics, Wasp was the one who gave Vision his name, shocked upon seeing him for the first time. In the film he's named by both Thor and Ultron. Thor refers to him as the "vision" he received in the form of a prophecy and Ultron refers to him as the object of his "vision" for the future.
Black Widow mentions in the movie that she was sterilized as part of final lesson of her training as a spy. Ironically, Scarlett Johansson was pregnant at the time of filming.

During Ultron's rage about being compared to Tony Stark, the disks/plates that make up his 'cheeks' seem to disappear, and then move back into position when he is confronted by Thor, Captain America and Iron Man. It is possible that when angered, these cheek plates retract to allow his jaw more articulation, mainly for expressing speech, and possibly as a nod to the open mouthed face of Ultron in the comics.
Long before the release of the movie, Joss Whedon said that Quicksilver and Scarlet Witch would not be immediate allies of The Avengers.
In the beginning of the movie, just as the Marvel logo fades out, you can briefly make out the shadow of Ant-Man, in his miniature form, as if he was in front of the Theater Projector Lens.
At the end of the film, Thor admits he's worried that four Infinity Stones have appeared already. This means Thor knows about the Guardians of the Galaxy retrieving the Orb from Ronan.
Hulk doesn't say a single word in this film.

In order for Iron Man to use his Mark XLIV/Hulkbuster, a satellite which Iron Man calls "Veronica", should launch the pod containing the Hulkbuster Armor, deploying itself around Iron Man. Another pod is deployed and follows the Hulkbuster during its battles. The floating and following pod contains spare and extra parts in order to replace certain damage or missing parts the Hulkbuster might face.

In the ending credits can be seen a brief scene where Thanos takes on a golden glove in his left hand and it says "Fine. I'll do it myself". This glove is in true the Infinity Gauntlet. In the homonymous comic published in 1990, Thanos used the Gauntlet to reunite the six Gems of Infinity, in order to increase his powers after receiving the mission to annihilate half of the population of the entire universe, which had been ordered by Mistress Death (the personification of death in the Marvel Universe).

Ultron's very first body (dubbed Ultron Mark 1) resembles a very worn out, heavily damaged endoskeletal Iron Legion drone. However his limbs appear very asymmetrical. This is because Ultron actually created that first body from the disassembled Iron Legion Drone 03 as well as using other parts, which accounts for the patchwork-esque look.
Ultron starts out as a peacekeeping force. This is a homage to The Avengers: Earth's Mightiest Heroes, where he had a similar origin.

When Scarlet Witch tries to mind control Hawkeye, he turns around and neutralizes her. He then quips: "I tried the mind control thing. Not a fan!" This is a reference to Jeremy Renner being openly displeased with his character being mind controlled by Loki during most of The Avengers.

An early script of movie was that Ultron was created by the government to eliminate the need of Avengers, but Ultron turns on its creators and then Avengers again team up to stop him. However, this draft was changed.

The Art of Avengers: Age of Ultron features a concept art image of Baron Strucker with the appearance of actor Vincent Cassel, suggesting that Cassel was intended to have a role in the film as Strucker before the actor Thomas Kretschmann was cast.
Age of Ultron is the only Avengers film not scored by Alan Silvestri.
Thor's vision features a statue of a kneeling Norseman. A smaller version of this statue appeared in Captain America: The First Avenger in a church in Norway.

Joss Whedon stated in an interview that he filmed an alternate version of the final scene in which Quicksilver wears an Avengers uniform and joins the new members of the team (in case Disney overruled his decision to kill the character).
Tim Roth revealed that his character, the Abomination, was slated to appear in the movie, before ultimately being shelved.
The post-credits caption promises "The Avengers will return".
Avengers: Age of Ultron is the most expensive comic book movie ever made.

This film was originally announced for a May 2, 2025 release, but initially delayed a year because of the writer and actor strikes in 2023, then pushed back further to December 18, 2026 to allow more time for production.
Avengers: Doomsday replaced the planned film Avengers: The Kang Dynasty as the predecessor to Avengers: Secret Wars.

In 2025, Channing Tatum revealed that he got injured while shooting a Gambit vs. Doctor Doom fight scene, resulting in him having to rely a lot on his stunt doubles and ADR dialogue to carry his appearance.

Compared to Thor: Love and Thunder, India Rose Hemsworth was much less cooperative on the set of this film, being more annoyed with having to do multiple takes while playing Love, and being upset that she wasn't being properly compensated. Chris Hemsworth had to promise her she'd get a motorbike and that she'd get to attend a Billie Eilish concert after wrapping filming to get her to perform her scenes.
The film marks the fifth Avengers movie, making the Avengers the longest running franchise in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Avengers: Endgame is the first MCU movie to feature all five founding members of the Avengers from their debut comic-book appearance in The Avengers #1 (Iron Man, Thor, Hulk and the original Ant-Man and Wasp). Loki, the team’s enemy in the issue, appears as well.

After retiring to his garden on the planet he called home, Thanos repurposed his discarded armor as a scarecrow. This is a direct reference to the ending of the Infinity Gauntlet comic miniseries, where Thanos similarly used his abandoned armor as a scarecrow in his garden after achieving his goal.

The storage unit where Scott Lang emerges from the Quantum Realm (and where Luis' Van is kept) is labeled number 616. This is a nod to Earth-616, the official designation for the primary/main continuity universe in Marvel Comics, where the majority of Marvel superhero stories take place.

Carol Danvers' updated appearance after the five-year time skip incorporates multiple elements from her comic book history: Her short hairstyle is taken directly from her modern comic book design, as is the red sash she wears as a belt; Her new predominantly red costume with black shoulder pads is modeled after the classic uniform of Captain Mar-Vell, the Kree hero from whom Carol inherited the "Captain Marvel" mantle.

During the holographic strategy meeting, Carol Danvers shows visible concern for James Rhodes and tells him to "be safe" before he departs on the Time Heist. This moment serves as a subtle nod to their romantic relationship in the comics, where the two characters (Captain Marvel and War Machine) have been in an on-and-off relationship since the mid-2010s, including periods around the Civil War II event and later storylines.

Thor's depressed, overweight appearance in the film is a nod to Walt Simonson's acclaimed Thor run. In the comics, Thor's brother Balder returned from Hela's realm deeply traumatized, coping by overeating and becoming fat and out of shape before eventually retraining himself.

The specialized suits worn by the Avengers to travel through and protect themselves in the Quantum Realm are similar in design and color scheme to the space suits worn by the Avengers in the animated series The Avengers: Earth's Mightiest Heroes.

The Mark 85 armor is a modernized yet largely faithful recreation of Iron Man's classic red-and-gold Mark II armor from the comics (his first iconic red and gold suit). Meanwhile, Captain America's new suit finally incorporates the classic "leafmail" chainmail design on the chest and shoulders, a hallmark of his traditional comic book costume. Additionally, the Mark 85 features a built-in energy shield that resembles the one Iron Man uses in the Marvel vs. Capcom video game series.

Barton was the first person after Scott Lang to enter the Quantum Realm by shrinking. This serves as a subtle nod to his time as the size-changing Goliath in the comics, where Clint Barton temporarily took on Hank Pym's growth powers and operated under that identity.

While planning the Time Heist with the Avengers, Rhodes suggests simply traveling back in time to kill Thanos as an infant, believing this would prevent the Snap from ever happening. This dark proposal alludes to Thanos Rising #1-#2, in which Thanos' mother, Sui-San, attempts to kill him the moment she sees him after his birth, sensing the monstrous future he would bring.

The central premise of the Avengers splitting into several smaller teams to travel through time — with heavy use of continuity porn referencing numerous past MCU events — appears to draw inspiration from Kurt Busiek's Avengers Forever miniseries. Marvel's official promotional sampler for new readers, released in conjunction with Endgame to encourage interest in the comics, listed Avengers Forever alongside the original Infinity Gauntlet miniseries as relevant stories.

During the elevator scene, Steve Rogers whispering "Hail Hydra" to Jasper Sitwell (and the other Hydra agents) in order to retrieve Loki's scepter is a direct reference to the Secret Empire comic event, in which Steve is revealed to be a Hydra sleeper agent and uses the phrase as his allegiance.

When Captain America faces an alternate version of himself during the Time Heist in 2012, it also serves as a nod to the comics' Secret Empire event, in which the real Steve Rogers battles his HYDRA-aligned doppelgänger (often called Hydra Cap or Hydra Supreme) for control of the shield and the fate of the heroes. Captain America fighting his past self is a direct reference to Captain America #156, which Steve Rogers battles the mentally unstable 1950s Captain America (an impostor who believes himself to be the "real" Cap)

In Hank Pym’s laboratory in 1970, a prototype of the Ant-Man Suit helmet is visible that closely resembles the character’s original helmet design from the comics. Also in 1970, an alternate Edwin Jarvis is seen talking with Howard Stark about his wife's pregnancy. Jarvis' brief cameo marks the first time that a character from a Marvel Television production appeared in a Marvel Studios production, being followed by Wilson Fisk/Kingpin in Hawkeye and Echo and Matt Murdock/Daredevil in Spider-Man: No Way Home, She-Hulk: Attorney at Law, and Echo. Fisk and Murdock will both appear in Daredevil: Born Again.

Nebula receives significantly more screentime and a pivotal role in the film, remaining instrumental in the plan against Thanos and ultimately contributing to his downfall. This is true to the comics, where Nebula plays a key part in Thanos' defeat in The Infinity Gauntlet by stealing the Infinity Gauntlet from him while he is distracted and using its power to reverse his actions.

When the Red Skull addresses Clint Barton on Vormir as "Clint, son of Edith", it contrasts with his references to Thanos (son of A'Lars), Gamora (daughter of Thanos), and Natasha (daughter of Ivan). This is a reference to Clint's comic book backstory, in which his father, Harold Barton, was an abusive alcoholic.

The "fight" between Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir for the Soul Stone, which requires the sacrifice of someone you love, references their turbulent and complicated romantic relationship in the comics.

Natasha's sacrifice on Vormir so that Clint can obtain the Soul Stone — which later allows him to be reunited with his family — is the direct inverse of Ultimates 2 #7, where the Ultimate Universe's Black Widow is responsible for the murder of Clint's wife and children.

Hulk sustaining severe damage to his right arm after using the Infinity Gauntlet is a reference to the Secret Wars comic event, in which the Hulk ends up with a broken limb (a leg, rather than an arm).

During the attack on the Avengers Compound, after the building is destroyed by Thanos' forces, the Hulk holds up a large piece of falling debris to protect Rocket and War Machine. This moment serves as a visual reference to the cover of Marvel Super Heroes Secret Wars #4, in which the Hulk lifts a massive boulder to shield several of his teammates from danger.

Tony Stark's line, "You mess with time, it tends to mess back," is a reference to the Age of Ultron comic event. In the storyline, an alternate version of Tony Stark delivers a similar warning to Wolverine and the Invisible Woman after their attempts to alter the past through time travel create unintended consequences and a worse future.

Thanos spins his Double-Edged Sword in front of himself like the rotor blades of a helicopter. This is possibly a subtle reference to the "Thanoscopter" from Spidey Super Stories #39, a memetic helicopter associated with the character in that children's comic series.

Captain America proves worthy of lifting and wielding Mjolnir. This is a reference to several instances in the comics where Steve Rogers has lifted Thor's hammer, including Thor #390, the What If? X-Men Age of Apocalypse #1, and Fear Itself #7.

Pepper Potts' Rescue armor is colored purple and silver. This color scheme originates from her appearance in the animated series Iron Man: Armored Adventures, rather than the red and silver Rescue armor seen in the comics.

Right before the Battle of Earth, Captain America shouts to the Avengers and their allies, "Avengers, assemble!". This is the team's iconic catchphrase in the comics, most commonly associated with Captain America himself.
