In the scene in which Phillips, Peggy and Captain America are chasing the Hydra plane in Schmidt's car, Phillips presses a red button, with the letter K on it and the German words Gefahr Nicht Drucken surrounding it which translates in English to "Danger Do Not Push", sending the car speeding faster down the runway. In the film Men in Black Tommy Lee Jones' character Kay warns his partner Jay (Will Smith) to never "ever touch the red button", and later in the film tells him to "push the little red button" sending their car speeding down a tunnel.

Paul Warren (an experienced film double and actor mostly known for roles wearing prosthetic) was used in pre-production to help develop the 'Skinny Steve Rogers' effect by CGI supervisor, Christopher Townsend, as well as one of the 'Skinny Steve' on set stand in's. English Shakespearean trained stage actor, Leander Deeny, was used on as the on set 'Skinny Steve' double when Chris Evans was sitting or lying down, or when a minimum of physical movement was required.
Samuel L. Jackson filmed a scene with Chris Evans for this movie in a modern New York City's Time Square which serve as a scene that preludes The Avengers.

Joe Johnston, the director of "Captain America: The First Avenger", also directed The Rocketeer. In the Rocketeer, the hero, Cliff Secord, finds a rocket pack created by Howard Hughes, thus becoming the Rocketeer. In Captain America: The First Avenger, Captain America obtains his iconic shield from Howard Stark, a character closely based on Howard Hughes.

There are several references to Raiders of the Lost Ark, which Director Joe Johnston worked on as Art Director: Red Skull's consumption at the hands of the Tesseract is very similar to how the Ark of the Covenant kills the Nazis; Captain America throws a Hydra pilot into a propeller; After he holds the Tesseract in his hands, Johann Schmidt makes a comment about how the Fuhrer "searches the desert for trinkets."

This is the last Marvel Studios film to use the original logo animation. A general Marvel logo would be used for The Avengers and Iron Man 3, and a new logo would be introduced in Thor: The Dark World.
Not counting his cameos in Thor: The Dark World or Spider-Man: Homecoming, this is the only film were Steve Rogers appears without Natasha Romanoff.

Martin T. Sherman portrayed Senator Brandt's aide, Senator Brandt himself was portrayed by Michael Brandon. The two had starred in the popular kids show Thomas & Friends together around the time this film released. Brandon was the narrator as well as the voice of Diesel, while Sherman voiced Thomas and Percy. Sherman stated in an interview that them meeting each other on the set of the film was pure coincidence and not an "in-joke" the directors did due to them working on Thomas together. He also stated that after their last scene filmed together, they went out for frozen yogurt to cement their friendship. Coincidentally, when Brandon left the show after 2012, Sherman became the voice of Diesel while still voicing Thomas and Percy. This was the case until Sherman left the show after 2014 due to disputes with Hit Entertainment.

William Hope (who portrayed one of the S.H.I.E.L.D. Lieutenants who were in the snow at the beginning) also starred in Thomas & Friends. He was the voice of Edward and Toby, as well as other characters during different seasons of the show, such as Bert. However, unlike Michael Brandon and Martin T. Sherman, William Hope remained on the show throughout its run.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Anthony Mackie described the film as "The Avengers: Part 1.5".

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Jasper Sitwell mentions Stephen Strange as a threat to Hydra. This small Easter egg foreshadows his eventual appearance in the MCU as Doctor Strange two years after this movie comes out.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Nick Fury mentions to Steve Rogers that the last time he trusted someone, he lost an eye. This foreshadows Fury losing his eye in the Captain Marvel film, which was released five years later.
The scene where Captain America jumps out of a plane without bothering to use a parachute is a homage to a similar scene from the first issue of "The Ultimates" comic.
Captain America's new costume takes cues from the "Super-Soldier" outfit he wore when he served as Director of S.H.I.E.L.D. in the comics.

The elevator fight with the STRIKE Team attempting to take Captain America prisoner is a homage to the Civil War story arc when Cap refuses to participate in the government's plan to register all superheroes and S.H.I.E.L.D. attempts to take him prisoner.
When Captain America and Black Widow use the secret elevator in the bunker, Cap uses his phone to detect the key code, and enters 8539. This is the date of Marvel Comics #1.
Maria Hill's last scene is of her joining Stark Industries. In the comics, she served under Tony Stark, but it was the other way around as he ended up joining S.H.I.E.L.D.
The film's plot is based on the storylines "The Winter Soldier" (Captain America's new threat) and "The Ultimates" (S.H.I.E.L.D. is taken over by Hydra).

The Winter Soldier was able to match Captain America move to move and even caught the iconic Shield of Captain America. This is a reference to the Winter Soldier taking up the mantle of Captain America, an event which has taken place in the comics.

For the scene in which Arnim Zola shows Steve Rogers and Natasha Romanoff the history of Hydra infiltrating S.H.I.E.L.D., the visual effects team originally created a file containing several names of characters from the comics, although it does not appear in the actual movie, including: Herrick Goldman, who worked with Wolverine and Maria Hill during the events of Civil War; E.B. Farrell, an expert marksman and elite S.H.I.E.L.D. agent nicknamed "Kid"; Rigby Fallon, who mainly appeared alongside Kitty Pryde, when she was an agent of S.H.I.E.L.D; John Allen Adams, who was secretly a part of Hydra; Earl Angstrom, an ally of the Michael Collins' version of Deathlok; Ted Bailey, who worked alongside another Deathlok, Jack Truman; Valeria Toomes, daughter of Adrian Toomes, aka the Vulture, in the comics. In the MCU she is merged with Liz Allan; Dino Manelli, a former Howling Commando who later became an agent of S.H.I.E.L.D; Daisy Johnson, better known as Quake, who previously appeared in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

Anna Kendrick, Felicity Jones, Imogen Poots, Teresa Palmer, Alison Brie, Emilia Clarke, Mary Elizabeth Winstead, Elizabeth Olsen and Jessica Brown Findlay were considered to play Sharon Carter. Jones would later be cast in The Amazing Spider-Man 2. Brown Findlay previously appeared in Iron Man 3 as the film used footage of her from television drama, Downton Abbey. Olsen portrayed Wanda Maximoff in the post credits scene of Captain America: The Winter Soldier, Avengers: Age of Ultron and Captain America: Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame, WandaVision and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Clarke would later play G'iah in Secret Invasion. Winstead would later play Helena Bartinelli/Huntress in the DC Extended Universe production Birds Of Prey.
Captain America: The Winter Soldier marks the second appearance together by Scarlett Johansson and Robert Redford, who previously appeared together in The Horse Whisperer, which Redford directed.
Captain America: The Winter Soldier is the first film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe to have two co-directors rather than one director.
Kevin Feige described the film as "a 1970s political thriller masquerading as a big superhero movie."
Principal photography began on April 1, 2013.

Captain America: The Winter Soldier marks the fourth time Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson have worked together, both starring in The Perfect Score (2004), The Nanny Diaries (2007) and The Avengers (2012).
Anthony Mackie was unhappy with the modern take on his costume as Falcon. He wanted the red spandex look from the comics.
In an attempt to prevent spoilers and maintain secrecy, the working title of the project while filming was "Freezer Burn."
Filming was done in Los Angeles, California, in Cleveland, Ohio and in Washington, D.C.
During filming, Sebastian Stan would walk around all day practicing his moves with a plastic knife because he wanted his movements to feel natural.

Captain America's uniform was altered from the ones seen in previous films, with a Kevlar-based ballistic component that would protect Captain America but at the same time function like a military uniform.
Filming in Cleveland began on May 17 and was scheduled to last until mid-June. It was concluded on June 27, 2013.
Cleveland was chosen as a stand-in for Washington, D.C., with the city's East 6th Street doubling for 7th and D Streets in Southwest D.C.
In several scenes, Natasha Romanoff wears a necklace with an arrow on it. This is a reference to her Avengers/S.H.I.E.L.D. teammate Hawkeye. The necklace was Scarlett Johansson's idea.
When Helicarriers look for their targets on one of the monitors there is a wire-frame model of the former Stark Tower in New York now sporting the Avengers symbol.
Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson wrote their own dialogue for several scenes they had together.

Anthony Mackie's appearance in this film fulfills his dream of playing a Marvel comic book character. He wrote a series of e-mail pleas to Marvel wanting to play any comic character that would appear on film. Though the studio repeatedly replied to him that they would respond in due time, Mackie's emails caught the attention of Kevin Feige, who subsequently offered him the role of Falcon.
Although playing a French/Algerian character, Georges St-Pierre speaks his lines in his native French-Canadian accent.

Black Widow mentions Operation Paperclip which is a real-world reference to the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) program in which over 1,500 German scientists, technicians, and engineers (such as Wernher von Braun, father of the V-2 and Saturn V rockets) from Nazi Germany and other foreign countries were brought to the United States for employment in the aftermath of World War II.
The filmmakers originally intended for Arnim Zola to transfer his consciousness into a robot and make an escape. This was scrapped for running time purposes.

A deleted scene explains why Captain America had to borrow his old uniform from the Smithsonian Institution: he let the STRIKE team track his new uniform to a basketball court while he went back to the hospital in regular clothes.
In Dr. Zola's lair, Black Widow says "Shall we play a game?" This is a line taken from WarGames which featured an intelligent supercomputer and a trigger to bomb specifically targeted locations.

When Steve enters his apartment through the window, a copy of Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein's non-fiction book All the President's Men is visible on his bookshelf. Robert Redford, played Bob Woodward in the 1976 movie adaptation.

Alexander Pierce's example of terrorists from Pakistan attacking Mumbai is a reference to the 2008 Mumbai attacks, when terrorists from Pakistan launched a series of attacks around places in Mumbai on the 26th of November, 2008.
A post-credits caption promises "Captain America will return in Avengers: Age of Ultron".
The elevator fight scene is parodied in Season 6, Episode 11 of the sitcom Community as a nod to the Russo Brothers, who frequently directed Community episodes.

This is the last MCU movie where Steve Rogers appears but Tony Stark doesn't appear at all. Every subsequent MCU film after this where Steve Rogers appears also features Tony Stark (excluding Steve Rogers' cameo appearance in the Captain Marvel post credit scene).

The movie marks the MCU debuts of Carol Danvers/Captain Marvel, Yon-Rogg, Talos, Mar-Vell, Maria Rambeau, Monica Rambeau, Minn-Erva, Att-Lass, Bron-Char, and the Supreme Intelligence. Other characters from the comics that appear in the movie are Joseph Danvers and Steve Danvers. The movie also adapts the character of Chewie the Cat, renamed Goose for the film.
The film also marks the MCU debut of the Skrulls. In the comics, the Skrulls are major players in the "Secret Invasion" and "Kree-Skrull War" storylines.
The film also features the MCU debut of Starforce and the Accuser Corps, which are both a part of the Kree Empire.
Between the many color variations Monica and Danvers test for the latter's suit, one of the options is a white-and-green variation, a reference to the Kree suits in the comics.

The movie takes the following elements from Kelly Sue DeConnick's time writing Captain Marvel: Making Yon-Rogg a primary antagonist;; Merging the characters of Maria Rambeau with Maria Renner, and;; Merging the characters of Katherine "Kit" Renner and Monica Rambeau.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Captain Marvel is Nick Fury's tenth live-action appearance, the others being, in chronological order, Iron Man, Iron Man 2, Thor, Captain America: The First Avenger, Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., The Avengers, Captain America: The Winter Soldier, Avengers: Age of Ultron and Avengers: Infinity War.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Kree make their fourth appearance in the MCU after Guardians of the Galaxy, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, and Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The film marks Phil Coulson's first appearance in a film since The Avengers. It also marks the second appearance of both Ronan the Accuser and Korath after Guardians of the Galaxy.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The honeycomb-shaped jump points make their second appearance following Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Nick Fury losing his eye to Goose was first referenced in Captain America: The Winter Soldier which was released four years earlier.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The film marks S.H.I.E.L.D.'s first appearance in a film since Avengers: Age of Ultron.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Transmitter Pager Fury used at the end of Avengers: Infinity War appears in the film, where it is revealed that it was created by S.H.I.E.L.D. in order to communicate, before being upgraded by Carol Danvers so Fury could contact her for emergencies.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: At the end of the film, the origins of the Avengers Initiative are revealed: After fighting in the Kree-Skrull War, Nick Fury realized that not even S.H.I.E.L.D. can defend Earth from extraterrestrial threats like the Kree, and, with Carol Danvers helping the Skrulls find a new home, Fury chose to find more heroes like her, to which he prepared what he named "The Protector Initiative", before changing its name to "The Avengers Initiative", in honor of Danvers' callsign.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Danvers meets the Avengers (Steve Rogers, Natasha Romanoff, Bruce Banner, and James Rhodes) in a mid-credits scene, which ties directly to the events of Avengers: Endgame.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In that scene, the Avengers are seen counting who died after the Snap, which occurred at the end of Infinity War.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Additionally, in that scene, the Avengers said that Fury activated the Transmitter Pager, which was seen in the post-credits scene of Infinity War.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: For the Quadjet scenes, Marvel Studios had to share a set made by Marvel Television for the TV series Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

During the Blockbuster scene, there are multiple 1990s movies referenced: Carol Danvers picks up a The Right Stuff VHS, nodding to her past in the Air Force; Carol destroys a True Lies standee. The filmmakers considered using a standee for The Mask instead, with Carol mistaking the green-faced Jim Carrey for a Skrull; Several VHS covers including ones for Junior, Hook, etc. are seen in the background; A theatrical poster for the 1995 Universal Pictures family film Babe can also be seen in the background.

There are several nods to Pulp Fiction. Talos sips a drink that is reminiscent from the one in the scene in the movie; The shot in which Nick Fury and Phil Coulson are in the car parallels the one in which John Travolta and Samuel L. Jackson do the same; The opening of the lunchbox to reveal the Tesseract mirrors the opening of the briefcase in this movie.
This is the third time that Brie Larson and Samuel L. Jackson starred in a movie after Kong: Skull Island and Unicorn Store.
This is the second film of the Marvel Cinematic Universe set entirely in the past and a prequel, the first being Captain America: The First Avenger.
This is Nicole Perlman's second time writing for a Marvel film. She previously wrote the first draft of Guardians of the Galaxy.
Jennifer Kent and Jennifer Yuh Nelson were in the running to direct the film.

Captain Marvel is the first female-led solo movie in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the first MCU movie to have a female director (Anna Boden), and the first MCU movie to have male and female directors.
The working title for the film is "Open World".

This film marks Stan Lee's first posthumous cameo in a Marvel Cinematic Universe film following his death in 2018. He is credited as playing himself and is seen reading the script for the 1995 film Mallrats, where he had a prominent cameo as himself. The Marvel Studios logo features a dedication to him. The concept art and film clip sections consist entirely of images of him, and the logo animation is followed by the message, "Thank you, Stan." Captain Marvel is the only MCU film released in 2019 to include the standard fanfare for the Marvel Studios logo.
A caption following the mid-credits scene promises Captain Marvel will return in Avengers: Endgame.

Captain Marvel is one of the only six MCU films not featuring Iron Man (along with Black Panther, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Spider-Man: No Way Home and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness) that grossed $1 billion and $900 million worldwide.

A scene in the film shows Carol Danvers using a computer that appears to be running Windows 98 Second Edition. This should be impossible, because the film takes place in 1995, and that operating system would not be released until spring of 1999.
Ronda Rousey had expressed interest in playing the title role.

Katheryn Winnick, Natalie Dormer, Emily Blunt, Katee Sackhoff, Yvonne Strahovski, and Rebecca Ferguson had been rumored for the title role before Brie Larson was cast. Dormer previously had a small role as Pvt. Lorraine in Captain America: The First Avenger.
Malaysian actress Raja Ilya was hinted to have a role in Captain Marvel.
Keanu Reeves originally was offered the role of Yon-Rogg but turned it down.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Roxxon Corporation, after having minor appearances throughout the Marvel Cinematic Universe, is featured extensively for the first time, as it shows up as an antagonist in the first season of Cloak & Dagger. Roxxon's competition with Stark Industries and Rand Enterprises is mentioned; Additionally, it is mentioned that Roxxon also operates in Pensacola. This is a reference to Roxxon's role in the events of Iron Man 3.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Darkforce, previously established in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. and Agent Carter, is featured in the show. The second season sees the Dark Dimension featured, with a specific domain inhabited by the Loa.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Brigid O'Reilly, who was mentioned in Luke Cage, references her times being in New York City, as well as her friend Misty Knight and Ben Urich.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The drink brand "O'Harren's Scotch Whisky" appears in both seasons of the show, after previously appearing in Agent Carter, Daredevil and The Punisher.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: A New York Bulletin article about Luke Cage written by Karen Page is shown and talked about.

Cloak & Dagger marks the debuts of Tyrone Johnson/Cloak and Tandy Bowen/Dagger in the MCU. Other characters adapted to Cloak & Dagger from comics include Brigid O'Reilly, Francis Xavier Delgado, Otis Johnson, Adina Johnson, Melissa Bowen, and Mister Jip. Season two added comics characters D'Spayre and Avandalia.
In First Light, Tandy Bowen uses a T-shirt that nods to the comic book counterpart of the famous British Band the Beatles, the Crick-Hits.
August D'Angelo is mentioned as Roxxon's CEO in an article shown in the episode Princeton Offense.

The show references elements from Vodu, such as Papa Legba and Baron Samedi. These two deities have been featured in Marvel Comics. The show also uses the song "the hymn to St. Brigid" which is a tribute to Maman Brigitte, as well as St. Bridget, the Irish Saint that Maman Brigitte comes from. Joe Pokaski has confirmed that it is also connected to Brigid O'Reilly.

Cloak & Dagger is the first MCU installment to have both male and female co-leads and have the names of two characters in the title, the second being Ant-Man and the Wasp. Coincidentally, both products were released in 2018.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: WHiH World News that covers the news regarding the bombings in Hell's Kitchen and all of Wilson Fisk's public appearances appeared previously in The Incredible Hulk, Iron Man 2, The Avengers, and Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: NY1 anchor Pat Kiernan appears as himself, which he previously did in The Avengers and Iron Man 3 and later did in Doctor Strange, The Defenders, The Punisher, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Hawkeye, and Spider-Man: No Way Home.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: According to Steven S. DeKnight, the scene where Stick reports the outcome of his mission to Stone was intended to be a post-credits scene, a recurring staple in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but it was simply added at the end of an episode due to the way Netflix airs its episodes.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: The Battle of New York and the events portrayed in The Avengers had changed New York City, with Leland Owlsley stating that "heroes and their consequences" are what made Wilson Fisk and his associates able to operate and make a profit from the situation.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: As a series of explosions strike in Hell's Kitchen, Elena Cardenas cries out in Spanish that the sky is falling down again, as another reference to the Battle of New York.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: New York Bulletin covered the news for the Battle of New York from The Avengers and the Duel of Harlem from The Incredible Hulk.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: In the episode In the Blood, James Wesley questions the reason a simple man in a mask is able to hijack Anatoly and Vladimir Ranskahov's operations, as if he had an iron suit or a magic hammer would explain it, referencing both Iron Man and Thor. Another Easter egg in this episode is the tattoo of the Ten Rings on Vladimir's arm during a flashback.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Claire Temple asks Matt Murdock in the episode World on Fire if he has a job or he is one of those "billionaire playboys", a reference to how Tony Stark likes to describe himself despite also acting as a superhero.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: Foggy Nelson mentioned Captain America in the episode Speak of the Devil.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Movies
facts.text: In the episode The Ones We Leave Behind there is a New York Bulletin article about Stark Tower.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
facts.text: Jack Murdock's opponent in his last boxing match is Carl Creel.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
facts.text: Following the death of his father, Matt Murdock was sent to Saint Agnes Orphanage, the same one where S.H.I.E.L.D. sent Skye following her retrieval from China.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
facts.text: In the episode The Ones We Leave Behind there is a New York Bulletin article about Cybertek.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
facts.text: The Dogs of Hell appeared in second season as one of the three criminal gangs involved in the shooting massacre in Central Park, that brought the death of Frank Castle's family.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.
facts.text: Cogmium steel, used by Kenji Oyama to replace Benjamin Poindexter's broken spine, was previously mentioned in A Wanted (Inhu)man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: New York Bulletin is a main organization in Daredevil. An article of NYB appeared for the first time in Agent Carter.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: The drink brand "O'Harren's Scotch Whisky" is also used in the show.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Agent Carter
facts.text: The Maggia is mentioned in the episode Upstairs/Downstairs. This criminal syndicate has ties to the Manfredi Crime Family which first appeared in Agent Carter.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Jessica Jones
facts.text: Jessica Jones is mentioned in Kinbaku and A New Napkin.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Jessica Jones
facts.text: Marci Stahl was hired by Hogarth, Chao & Benowitz after she left Landman and Zack. She also introduced Foggy Nelson to her new employee Jeri Hogarth, who was impressed by his closing statement during the trial of Frank Castle.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Jessica Jones
facts.text: Brett Mahoney quoted Oscar Clemons in the episode Dogs to a Gunfight.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Jessica Jones
facts.text: Claire Temple paid the consequences from helping Luke Cage and Jessica Jones leaving Metro-General Hospital without regular permissions in the episode AKA Smile.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Iron Fist
facts.text: Set photos of Into the Ring reveal that the chemicals that blinded Matt Murdock were manufactured by Rand Enterprises.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Iron Fist
facts.text: In The Ones We Leave Behind, Madame Gao indirectly refers to K'un-Lun, mentioning her homeland.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Iron Fist
facts.text: In Kinbaku, an article on the New York Bulletin refers to a "mysterious lost city" which could be another reference to K'un-Lun.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / Iron Fist
facts.text: The Yangsi Gonshi and Golden Tigers are mentioned in the episode Upstairs/Downstairs.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe / The Defenders
facts.text: The Destruction of Midland Circle was referenced several times in the third season. Also, the scene with Matt Murdock in Saint Agnes Orphanage recreates the last scene of The Defenders.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Marvel Characters
facts.text: Characters from Marvel Comics adapted into the show as the main cast: Matt Murdock/Daredevil, Karen Page, Foggy Nelson, James Wesley, Ben Urich, Leland Owlsley, Vanessa Marianna, Claire Temple and Wilson Fisk/Kingpin in the first season; Frank Castle/Punisher, Elektra and Blake Tower in the second season; Benjamin Poindexter/Bullseye and Margaret Murdock in the third season.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Marvel Characters
facts.text: Other characters from Marvel Comics adapted into the show: Stick, Jack Murdock, Paul Lantom, Melvin Potter, Turk Barrett, Nobu Yoshioka, Brett Mahoney, Stone, Don Rigoletto, Roscoe Sweeney, Sammy Silke, Randolph Cherryh, Josie, Doris Urich, Joseph Pike and Stewart Schmidt in the first season; Grotto, Hirochi, Nesbitt, Maria Castle, Lisa Castle, Frank Castle, Jr., Nesbitt, Finn Cooley, Ray Schoonover, Star, Benjamin Donovan and Max in the second season; Felix Manning, Edward Nelson, Anna Nelson, Betsy Beatty, Paxton Page, Michael Kemp and Kenji Oyama in the third season.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Marvel Characters
facts.text: Leland Owlsley talks about two businessmen from the comics in regards to the gala hosted by Wilson Fisk. The one he wanted in the guest list despite knowing he would not come is a reference to Richmond, who could be a reference to Kyle Richmond, an arrogant rich boy until he assumed the code name Nighthawk and became a member of the Defenders; while the one who helped Randolph Cherryh with his election through astrology is a reference to Cornelius van Lunt, a member of the Great Wheel of the Zodiac who assumed the codename Taurus and formed the Zodiac Cartel. The words Van Lunt are also painted on the door to Nelson and Murdock's office.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Marvel Characters
facts.text: Melvin Potter's workshop has many references to his identity as the Gladiator in the comics, such as the symbol of his costume being present in one of his designs, blueprints for his buzz-saw arm weapons and a poster for a movie, Revenge of the Gladiators. It also has references for another villain Stilt-Man, by having buzz saws created by Kaxton Industries, and the set of legs used in the Stilt-Man Suit. By Season Two, the suit seems to be updated and the torso completed.

facts.section: References to Marvel Comics / Marvel Characters
facts.text: Though not directly derived from the comics, John Healy, a hitman that killed one of its victims in a bowling alley crushing his victim's skull with a bowling ball, shares his last name with Elton Healy and Alvin Healy, two brothers and costumed criminals. Alvin used bowling tenpins as throwing weapons, matching the scene depicted in the TV series.
Daredevil's first outfit is inspired by one of Frank Miller's stories, The Man Without Fear.
Matt Murdock's alias as "Mike" is an homage to the storyline where he had to pose as his own twin brother "Mike Murdock" to deflect suspicion from him being Daredevil.
Ben Urich mentions having investigated Karen Page's past activities, which in the comics involve drugs and pornography.
The colors of the vest that Melvin Potter creates for Leland Owlsley are the same ones used by his Owlsley's comic counterpart as Owl.
Vanessa Marianna explains to Wilson Fisk she once dated a man in a white suit and an ascot, which is Fisk's usual outfit in the comics.
Dutton refers to Fisk's nickname "Kingpin" in the episode Seven Minutes in Heaven.
Elektra's death accidental by the hands of Nobu Yoshioka is very similar to her death in the comics, where she was killed by Bullseye with her own sai.

Benjamin Poindexter adopting Daredevil's suit and persona in order to frame him is a loose reference to the Daredevil: Born Again storyline, where Kingpin let a mental patient loose wearing a Daredevil costume in order to kill Foggy Nelson.
Benjamin Poindexter's apartment number is 131. This is a reference to Bullseye's first appearance in Daredevil #131.
Benjamin Poindexter's baseball cap with bullseye insignia is a reference to his comic appearance.

In A New Napkin, Poindexter was operated on his spine by Kenji Oyama. In the comics, Bullseye is also given a metal spine (but instead of being cogmium steel, it is adamantium) that is also given to him Kenji Oyama, aka. Lord Dark Wind.

Punisher was originally set to be introduced in a post-credits scene at the end of Daredevil, where he kills Leland Owlsley, with the character's face unseen but his skull insignia appearing. But the idea was dropped because the way Netflix airs its series episodes.

In Dogs to a Gunfight, Frank Castle and an elderly man named Jerry, both former members of the United States Marine Corps, have a chat about their military carriers. While Castle served in Iraq and Afghanistan, Jerry talks about his military service in the Vietnam War. This is a reference to the original Punisher from the comics, who served in Vietnam as well before his backstory was updated in recent times.
The first four digits of Frank Castle's trial are 1986, the year of the release of the first Punisher comic book series.
The term Warzone is used multiple times throughout the second season to describe Frank Castle's actions, a reference to The Punisher War Zone comic book series.
In Regrets Only, Elektra refers to Matt Murdock as "Mr. Magoo". This is a nickname often used by Spider-Man for Daredevil.
In One Last Shot, a poster in Fogwell's Gym advertises a boxing match between Parker and Morales, nodding to both versions of Spider-Man, Peter Parker and Miles Morales.

Asano Robotics, the company used to bring Black Sky to New York City, is a reference to the company created Yoshida Asano to create a suit of armor and get revenge on Tony Stark for Howard Stark's work on the Manhattan Project.
Atreus Plastics and Summerville Department Stores, two companies from the comics, are pictured in the last episode of the first season, Daredevil, on the trucks who moved Wilson Fisk away.
A truck owned by Redfield Electronics, a company owned by Jim Redfield in the comics, was stolen by the Dogs of Hell and later used by Frank Castle as a distraction in an ambush.

Drew Goddard had originally pitched a Daredevil project to Marvel Studios as a two-film series, with the first film focusing on Kingpin and the second film featuring Punisher as their respective villains. Marvel initially turned down the pitch due to not being interested in producing R-rated content for the Marvel Cinematic Universe at the time, leading Goddard to convert his planned films into the television series.
Michael C. Hall was rumored to play Daredevil. The actor had expressed consideration in playing the part.
According to Jeph Loeb, Joe Quesada wanted Charlie Cox to play Daredevil even before Marvel Studios regained the rights to adapt the comic.

This is the first Marvel Television series where Stan Lee does not make a cameo appearance. However, his image appears in the first season finale in a portrait as a cop in the 15th Precinct Police Station.

Drew Goddard was initially hired as the showrunner, but had to withdraw because of his writing commitment to The Martian, which released later the same year as season one, as well as his directing commitment to the eventually-caneled The Sinister Six, another Marvel property owned by Sony Pictures Entertainment. Goddard remained on as a consultant while Steven S. DeKnight was hired as a replacement.

The title of episode 1.01, Into the Ring, is a reference to Matt Murdock's rise as a vigilante opposite to Wilson Fisk and his allies, being compared to a new boxer stepping into the ring against his opponent and also Jack Murdock, a boxer himself.

The title of episode 1.02, Cut Man, is a reference to the wounds Daredevil sustains during the episode, and also to the assassination of Jack Murdock for not giving up his fight against Carl Creel, thus being cut from Roscoe Sweeney's schemes.
The title of episode 1.03, Rabbit in a Snowstorm, is a reference to the painting that Wilson Fisk stared at the end of the episode, that was described for him by Vanessa Marianna.
The title of episode 1.04, In the Blood, is a reference to Wilson Fisk telling Vanessa Marianna that New York City is a part of him and "in his blood," which he claims is his drive to make it better.

The title of episode 1.05, World on Fire, is a reference to the way that Matt Murdock describes how he sees the world, and also to the series of explosions in Hell's Kitchen that are caused in the episode.
The title of episode 1.06, Condemned, is a reference to the hunt of Daredevil and Vladimir Ranskahov by the police throughout the episode.
The title of episode 1.07, Stick, is a reference to Matt Murdock's old mentor, Stick, who reappears in his life during the episode.

The title of episode 1.08, Shadows in the Glass, is a reference to the reflection of the past that hunts Wilson Fisk, and that often sees reflected in his own mirror as a younger and bloodied version of himself.

The title of episode 1.09, Speak of the Devil, is a reference to the idiom Speak of the devil and he doth appear, used when an object of discussion unexpectedly becomes present during a conversation. It could be a reference to the sudden appearance of Wilson Fisk after the duel between Daredevil and Nobu Yoshioka. Fisk was also referred to as "the Devil" in a conversation between Matt Murdock and Father Paul Lantom, during the episode.
The title of episode 1.10, Nelson v. Murdock, is a reference to the conflict between Foggy Nelson and Matt Murdock brought in the episode, and written in the same style as used in trials.

The title of episode 1.11, The Path of the Righteous, is a reference to Father Paul Lantom's suggestion Matt Murdock that the Devil's existence is a sign for all men to tread "the path of the righteous."

The title of episode 1.12, The Ones We Leave Behind, is a reference to Ben Urich's death by the end of the episode, and possibly to all the other friends and allies of Matt Murdock, Foggy Nelson and Karen Page whose lives were forsaken in their search for justice, like Daniel Fisher and Elena Cardenas.

The title of episode 1.13, Daredevil, is a reference to what the newspapers and the general public decided to call the man in the mask after he defeated Wilson Fisk. It also references the first time in the series Matt puts on his red suit, which is closer in appearance to the classic Daredevil suit from the comics.
The title of episode 2.01, Bang, is a reference to the first word spoken by the Punisher in the series, when he shoots Daredevil in the forehead at the end of the episode.

The title of episode 2.02, Dogs to a Gunfight, is a play to the idiom "don't take a knife to a gunfight", usually referred when someone enters a fight without being adequately equipped. This is a reference to the New York City Police Department's ambush to the Punisher, that whose easily outmatched by the vigilante. It also a reference to Punisher's dog, Max, who also appears in the episode.

The title of episode 2.03, New York's Finest, is a slang term referred to the New York City Police Department, usually in a depreciative way, as a group of people who put themselves above the Law. This definition applied to both Daredevil and the Punisher.
The title of episode 2.04, Penny and Dime, is a reference to "One Batch, Two Batches, a Penny and Dime", Lisa Castle's favorite nursery rhyme repeated by the Punisher before every shot.

The title of episode 2.05, Kinbaku, is a reference to a japanese style of bondage used for artistic or sexual purposes. In the episode's flashbacks, Roscoe Sweeney was tied by Elektra following the principles of the Kinbaku.
The title of episode 2.06, Regrets Only,.
The title of episode 2.07, Semper Fidelis, is a reference to United States Marine Corps's motto.
The title of episode 2.08, Guilty as Sin,.

The title of episode 2.09, Seven Minutes in Heaven, is a reference to the party game "Seven minutes in heaven". In the episode, Frank Castle had seven minutes to move in Block A in Rikers Island to gain the information he wanted from Dutton.
The title of episode 2.10, The Man in the Box,.
The title of episode 2.11,.380, is a reference to Karen Page's gun, a Llama III-A.380 model pistol.
The title of episode 2.12, The Dark at the End of the Tunnel, is a play to the idiom "the light at the end of the tunnel"

The title of episode 2.13, A Cold Day in Hell's Kitchen, is a reference to the play a Cold Day in Hell, indicating something that would never happen under any circumstances. The title also referred to the episode ending on Christmas Day, and it forms a symmetry with the beginning of the season, who started in a 100 F°-hot day.
The title of episode 3.01, Resurrection, is a reference to Matt Murdock resuming his vigilante activities as Daredevil after recovering from injuries he sustained at the end of The Defenders.
The title of episode 3.02, Please, is a reference to the prayers Matt Murdock would hear at church while growing up, interpreting this as God telling him to answer them.

The title of episode 3.03, No Good Deed, is a reference to the phrase "no good deed goes unpunished"', referring to Wilson Fisk getting released from prison in spite of Daredevil's actions to bring him to justice.

The title of episode 3.04, Blindsided, is a reference to Matt Murdock getting caught off guard by the attack Wilson Fisk planned for him at Rikers Island, as well as being a reference to his blindness.
The title of episode 3.05, The Perfect Game, is a reference to Benjamin Poindexter's desire as a child to pitch a perfect game to bring his parents back.

The title of episode 3.06, The Devil You Know, is a reference to the saying "better the devil you know than the devil you don't"'. Ironically, the Daredevil suit in the episode is worn by Benjamin Poindexter, who is not "the devil you know."
The title of episode 3.07, Aftermath, is a reference to the aftermath of "Daredevil's" attack on the New York Bulletin.

The title of episode 3.08, Upstairs/Downstairs, is a reference to Daredevil escaping Benjamin Poindexter's attacks by going upstairs on the fire escape, and hearing Maggie Grace's prayer downstairs confirming she is his mother.

The title of episode 3.09, Revelations, is a reference to Father Paul Lantom's revelations to Matt Murdock about Maggie Grace being his mother, as well as Ray Nadeem learning that numerous agents at the FBI are already working for Wilson Fisk.
The title of episode 3.10, Karen, is a reference to Karen Page, as a large part of the episode is dedicated to her backstory.
The title of episode 3.11, Reunion, is a reference to Matt Murdock, Karen Page and Foggy Nelson reuniting together for the first time in the season.
The title of episode 3.12, One Last Shot, is a reference to everyone's desparation to have Ray Nadeem testify against Wilson Fisk in front of a jury, to take him down the legal way.
The title of episode 3.13, A New Napkin, is a reference to a napkin Foggy Nelson uses to draft a name for a new law firm with Matt Murdock and Karen Page.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: In the series premiere Heaven's Half Hour, Foggy Nelson references his former employment at Hogarth, Chao & Benowitz to Kirsten McDuffie.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: While conversing with Matt Murdock at Square Diner in Heaven's Half Hour, Wilson Fisk mentions a past attempt to mentor someone, referencing Maya Lopez. Murdock alludes to how she shot Fisk in the face, gesturing towards the events of the Hawkeye episode So This Is Christmas? In the same conversation, Fisk reflects on the death of Foggy Nelson and acknowledges the promise he made not to expose Murdock's secret identity, nor target either Nelson or Karen Page, following his defeat at the Presidential Hotel in the Daredevil series finale A New Napkin.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Wilson Fisk's televised speech commemorating his election to Mayor of New York City references Spider-Man with regards to addressing his intent to curb vigilante activities within the city, alongside Daredevil and the Punisher in Heaven's Half Hour.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: A billboard advertisement for Rogers: The Musical is seen in an establishing shot of Times Square in the episode Optics. Also seen in the same shot is an advertisement for Harlem's Paradise, the nightclub run by Luke Cage.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Yusuf Khan, featured previously in The Marvels and Ms. Marvel, appears in the episode With Interest. Kamala Khan is also referenced in the episode, and the family photo of Yusuf, Kamala, Muneeba Khan, and Aamir Khan is shown.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Skrulls are mentioned in the episode Sic Semper Systema, having previously had their existence made public in Secret Invasion.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: FXN, previously featured in both Daredevil and Secret Invasion, makes an appearance in both seasons' premiere episodes.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: From off-screen, Valentina Allegra de Fontaine makes a phone call to Alan Steverud while he meets with Wilson Fisk at New York City Hall during the second season premiere episode The Northern Star, successfully persuading him to pledge support for the Safer Streets Initiative and enable him to conduct his policies without broader federal oversight.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Watchtower, the main base of operations for the New Avengers, appears in establishing shots of New York City in the second season episodes The Northern Star, Gloves Off, and The Hateful Darkness, having completed construction since the events of Thunderbolts*.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Ben Urich's office at New York Bulletin is shown in the second season finale The Southern Cross, featuring some of his newspaper articles from Daredevil. The articles also serve as references to the Battle of New York from The Avengers, the Duel of Harlem from The Incredible Hulk, Tony Stark and Stark Tower, and Cybertek from Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..
Vanessa Fisk, previously portrayed by Ayelet Zurer in Daredevil, was recast and portrayed by Sandrine Holt, who was later recast back to Zurer.
This is Michael Gaston's second role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe following his role as Gerald Sharpe in the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. episode Alien Commies from the Future!.
This is Clark Johnson's first role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe following his contributions as a director for the two Luke Cage episodes You Know My Steez and For Pete's Sake.
Production on Daredevil: Born Again was delayed due to the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike.
The title of episode 1.01, Heaven's Half Hour, is a reference to Josie's toast to Cherry, as well as the brief celebration and bliss for Nelson, Murdock & Page before Bullseye attacked Josie's Bar.

The title of episode 1.02, Optics, is a reference to Sheila Rivera explaining to Wilson Fisk the importance of optics in his first few days in office. The title may also be a reference to Matt Murdock's blindness.
The title of episode 1.03, The Hollow of His Hand, is a reference to Heather Glenn's toast to Matt Murdock on the verdict to The People v. Hector Ayala.
The title of episode 1.04, Sic Semper Systema, is a play on the Latin phrase "Sic semper tyrannis" ("thus always to tyrants"), instead referencing Matt Murdock's waning faith in the justice system.
The title of episode 1.05, With Interest, is a reference to the financial concept of interest, as the episode takes place in New York Mutual Bank.

The title of episode 1.06, Excessive Force, is a reference to Mayor Wilson Fisk enlisting corrupt cops into his Anti-Vigilante Task Force, as well as Matt Murdock resuming his activities as the vigilante Daredevil, thus both of them returning to using "excessive force."
The title of episode 1.07, Art for Art's Sake, is a reference to Muse making paintings and murals through killing people, thus making art "for art's sake."
The title of episode 1.08, Isle of Joy, is a reference to the lyrics in the song Manhattan, which played during Fisk's Black & White Ball.

The title of episode 1.09, Straight to Hell, is a reference to Mayor Wilson Fisk escalating his Anti-Vigilante Campaign by authorizing a blackout over New York City, breeding chaos and sending it "straight to hell." It is also a reference to Daredevil returning to Hell's Kitchen after quitting one year prior.
The title of episode 2.01, The Northern Star, is a reference to the ship of the same name featured within the episode.
The title of episode 2.02, Shoot the Moon, is a reference to a quote by Connor Powell about wanting to capture Matt Murdock and Daredevil.
The title of episode 2.03, The Scales & The Sword, is a reference to the scales of justice being rigged against Swordsman during his trial, as well as his alias and weapon of choice.

The title of episode 2.04, Gloves Off, is a reference to the boxing match between Wilson Fisk and Matterhorn, as well as the events of the episode leading the former to "take his gloves off" and return to his ruthless ways.

The title of episode 2.05, The Grand Design, is a reference to the "grand design" that led to Daredevil rescuing Bullseye after trying to kill him before, and the "grand design" that led to Vanessa Fisk meeting Wilson Fisk.
The title of episode 2.06, Requiem, is a reference to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's Requiem playing during Vanessa Fisk's funeral, as well as the conflict New York City escalating in wake of her death.
The title of episode 2.07, The Hateful Darkness, is a reference to Daredevil expressing his hatred to Bullseye for all the people he killed, and part of him wanting to kill him for that.

The title of episode 2.08, The Southern Cross, is a reference to the constellation of the same name, contrasting the title of the season's first episode, The Northern Star. The southern cross may also be a reference to Matt Murdock's life turning upside down after the events of the episode.
Daredevil: Born Again is a sequel series to the show Daredevil, and as of 2026, is the only sequel series within the MCU.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: When confronted by Hulk in an alternate Wolverine's universe, Deadpool begins saying he is Marvel Jesus and calls Hulk a "dull creature" before he is swiped away by the behemoth, referencing how Loki said he was a god and called Hulk a dull creature in The Avengers.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Deadpool and Wolverine get shawarma after destroying the Time Ripper and defeating Cassandra Nova and Mr. Paradox, similar to how the Avengers got shawarma after the Battle of New York in The Avengers.

The opening intro's song "Bye Bye Bye" by NSYNC was featured in X2: X-Men United, when Pyro turns on the radio in Cyclops' car and Wolverine annoyingly turns it off. Way back in Deadpool 2, NYSNC was suggested to call by Deadpool after Celine Deon's performs Ashes.
In Deadpool 2, The music box has Logan's corpse, in Logan is the burial grave where Laura buried Logan, and in the movie is where Deadpool desecrated to exhume Logan's skeleton.
A certain part of the fight choreography of the Duel in the Void is an exact recreation of the fight between Peter Parker and Flash Thompson in Spider-Man.
Blade says that "some motherfuckers [were] still trying to ice skate uphill", a line he originally said in Blade.

When Deadpool gets Nicepool killed due to the latter not having a healing factor, Wolverine calls Deadpool God's perfect idiot, which is what Deadpool was called in the opening credits of 20th Century Fox's Deadpool.
Deadpool mentions Scoutmaster Kevin, a character he originally mentioned in Deadpool 2.

Blade says he doesn't like Deadpool, to which Deadpool responds that he never did, referring to Wesley Snipes. This a reference to the fact that Snipes and Ryan Reynolds did not enjoy working together on Blade: Trinity.

Deadpool attempts to console Elektra about the death of her world's Daredevil at the hands of Cassandra Nova, to which she replies, "It's fine." This is a joke simultaneously referencing the 20th Century Fox film Daredevil, which starred Ben Affleck as Matt Murdock alongside Jennifer Garner as Elektra, and the relationship between the two co-stars that emerged from their work together on the film which ended when the pair divorced in 2018.
Deadpool and his friends celebrate his return by eating Feige's Famous Pizza, a pizza place that Deadpool ordered from in Deadpool.

During the credits, a montage of footage and archive footage from Marvel movies made by 20th Century Fox is shown to honor the legacy of those movies. Featured in the montage includes Hugh Jackman as Wolverine, Patrick Stewart as Professor X, Ian McKellen as Magneto, Halle Berry as Storm, James Marsden as Cyclops, Chris Evans as Human Torch, Jennifer Garner as Elektra, Scott Adkins as Weapon XI, James McAvoy as Professor X, Anna Paquin as Rogue, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique, Jennifer Lawrence as Mystique, Stan Lee, Kelly Hu as Lady Deathstrike, Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler, Kodi Smit-McPhee as Nightcrawler, Liev Schreiber as Sabretooth, Tyler Mane as Sabretooth, Jessica Alba as Invisible Woman, Ryan Reynolds as Weapon XI and Deadpool, Ben Affleck as Daredevil, Jon Favreau as Foggy Nelson, Brian Cox as William Stryker, Michael Fassbender as Magneto, Vinnie Jones as Juggernaut, Famke Janssen as Jean Grey, Doug Jones as Silver Surfer, Tye Sheridan as Cyclops, Aaron Stanford as Pyro, Michael B. Jordan as Human Torch, Dafne Keen as X-23, Nicholas Hoult as Beast, Miles Teller as Mister Fantastic, Michael Chiklis as Thing, Jamie Bell as Thing, Sophie Turner as Phoenix, Evan Peters as Quicksilver, and Oscar Isaac as Apocalypse.

Cavillrine unleashes his claws by pumping or "reloading" his arms, mimicking Henry Cavill's character in Mission: Impossible – Fallout, August Walker, doing the same motion in preparation for a fight.
The Nakatomi Plaza from Die Hard is present among the stuff that had been pruned to the Void by the Time Variance Authority.
The Chrysler LeBaron from Planes, Trains and Automobiles is present among the stuff that had been pruned to the Void by the Time Variance Authority.

Deadpool asks Dogpool who she wants to be her owner: the "original recipe", referring to himself, or "Van Milder," referring to Nicepool. This is a reference to the film Van Wilder, in which Ryan Reynolds portrayed the titular character.

Deadpool puts his hand on the glass of the door to the matter and anti-matter chamber in a manner that called back the way Spock placed a Vulcan salute on a chamber door in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan.
Nicepool says “the proposal” to the audience during the confrontation with the Deadpool Corps, The Proposal was another movie Ryan Reynolds starred in.

Deadpool & Wolverine is the first Marvel Cinematic Universe film to serve as a sequel to a non-MCU film based on Marvel Comics characters, as Deadpool and Deadpool 2 are part of the X-Men film series produced by 20th Century Fox.
This is the first MCU film where none of the main characters originate from the MCU Universe. This is also the first Deadpool film to be officially set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

This film is the first ever MCU film to target an "R" (Restricted 18+) rating from the Motion Picture Association of America, in line with the prior two Deadpool films. It is also the second MCU movie to drop the f-bomb uncensored, following Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, in which Star-Lord dropped it at Nebula while telling her to open the car door.
This is the first Deadpool film to not feature T.J. Miller as Weasel in any capacity.

Multiple titles were considered for the film, originally named Deadpool 3, during shooting including Deadpool vs. Wolverine, Deadpool & Wolverine (which ended up being the film's title) and Deadpool 3 with Wolvie.
Hugh Jackman said "Fuck Yeah!" when he tried the iconic Wolverine Suit for the first time.
A crucial scene from the film was supposed to be a shot-for-shot recreation of Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader's final duel from Return of the Jedi.

In response to a series of set leaks from the film, Ryan Reynolds posted humorously edited versions of the set leaks. Edits include adding a Predator, Mickey Mouse and Steve Urkel to certain photos and replacing the 20th Century Fox logo with the logo of Quibi.
In the movie, the comic book Secret Wars #5 can be seen next to Deadpool in the Void before he is met by an angry Wolverine.

Vinnie Jones, who played Cain Marko/Juggernaut in X-Men: The Last Stand, rejected an offer to reprise the role in Deadpool & Wolverine over complaints regarding the suit and the lack of budget for it from Marvel Studios.

Karan Soni revealed that the original story for Deadpool & Wolverine back when it was being developed as Deadpool 3 at 20th Century Fox similarly brought back Wolverine but involved Deadpool traveling to the North Pole to save Christmas.
The film has been announced to contain lots of "Kevin Feige jokes".

Famke Janssen, who played Jean Grey/Dark Phoenix in the X-Men film series, has declined to be in the film after being asked about whether she will reprise her role or not in the film several times beforehand.

Deadpool & Wolverine features Dogpool making it the second MCU project that includes an animal variant of a character. The first project to include this was Loki, which featured Alligator Loki and Throg.
Deadpool & Wolverine features Kidpool, making it the second MCU project that includes an kid variant of a character. The first project to include this was Loki, which featured Kid Loki.
Deadpool & Wolverine is the first MCU film in which a director/writer and a star/writer receive full producer credits.

Disney+ released a green band version of the official teaser for Deadpool & Wolverine with a few notable differences, including: An added scene with Peter Wisdom carrying Wade Wilson's birthday cake before setting it on a table; Wade Wilson says "The R-rating isn't new for me" instead of "Pegging isn't new for me" before he is arrested by TVA Minutemen; This scene, involving Rob McElhenney (a friend of Ryan Reynolds) playing said Minuteman, was later cut entirely from the film; Deadpool yells "OMG" instead of "Oh my fuck" after witnessing a Minuteman being snatched from the ground by Alioth.

The establishment Liefield's Just Feet is a reference to Deadpool creator Rob Liefeld, who has a reputation of being bad at drawing feet. In July 2023, Liefeld approved the joke before it was included in the movie.

Ryan Reynolds' original pitch for Deadpool & Wolverine was rejected by Kevin Feige as he wasn't sure how to incorporate Deadpool in the MCU. Reynolds pitched at least 25 different versions of Deadpool & Wolverine.

Kevin Feige initially told Hugh Jackman to not return as Wolverine after the character's death in Logan. However, Feige was onboard for Jackman reprising the role after it was decided he would not be playing the same variant of Wolverine he played in the Fox X-Men series.

On May 30, 2024, Ryan Reynolds revealed on X that a popcorn bucket had been created for the film that resembled Wolverine's head, with popcorn being poured into his mouth. He declared that 2024 would be remembered as the year that the War of the Popcorn Buckets began, referencing the infamous popcorn bucket created for the release of Dune: Part Two, which was modeled after a Sandworm and inspired many jokes that it would be used as a sex toy.

Following the announcement of Disney shifting physical media distribution to Sony Pictures Home Entertainment, this is the first Marvel Studios feature film to not be distributed by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment on physical media in North America.
During the early development of Deadpool & Wolverine, Mephisto was one of the antagonists considered for the film.
The fact that Ladypool had recently had a baby in the film is a reference to the fact that Blake Lively, the actress who portrayed Ladypool, had recently had a baby.
Deadpool told a Minuteman to "get [his] country's name out [his] fucking mouth", a reference to what Will Smith told Chris Rock at the 94th Academy Awards after the former slapped the latter.
Channing Tatum wanted to take Gambit's costume with him at the end of filming, as he had done on his previous films, but was too scared to do so.

While this movie primarily serves a farewell tribute to mostly Fox-produced Marvel movies, Wesley Snipes' Blade, an alternate Punisher and an variant of Russian are the only characters who are neither from Marvel Cinematic Universe Prime, nor from alternate universe movies produced by 20th Century Fox in this movie. Blade's case is from New Line, which is now merge into Warner Bros. Pictures. Although it is unknown which alternate version of Punisher referred in this movie, due to the character being dead prior to the main event, while Russian is confirmed to be a Variant of the one from Earth-58732.
A "What's up, Doc?" line spoken by Gambit is a reference to iconic greetings spoken by Bugs Bunny from Warner Bros.' Looney Tunes.
In order to get Dogpool to lick Deadpool's mouth, Ryan Reynolds put salmon paste on his lips.
Director by Night was directed by Anthony Giacchino, who is the brother of Werewolf by Night director Michael Giacchino.
It involves most of the Giacchino family.
Director by Night replaces Assembled as a documentary for Werewolf by Night.

facts.section: Reference to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Wong makes a comparison between the Masters of the Mystic Arts and the Avengers to Stephen Strange, specifying that they are battling more mystical threats from extra-dimensional beings.

facts.section: Reference to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Avengers Tower can be seen on the New York City skyline.

facts.section: Reference to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Near the end of the movie, Wong reveals that the Eye of Agamotto contains an Infinity Stone. This is the fifth Infinity Stone revealed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

facts.section: Reference to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Guidebook to the Marvel Cinematic Universe - Doctor Strange reveals that Stephen Strange and Christine Palmer worked at Metropolitan General Hospital, which is also called Metro-General Hospital. This hospital franchise was introduced in Daredevil, and later appeared in Jessica Jones and Iron Fist.

Characters from the movie adapted from the comics in the main cast are Stephen Strange/Doctor Strange, the Ancient One, Karl Mordo, Kaecilius, Christine Palmer, Wong and Dormammu. Other characters from the comics are Nic West, Daniel Drumm and Hamir. A character based on Tina Minoru, named in the credits only, has a cameo appearance in the film. Minoru later appeared in Runaways and played by Brittany Ishibashi, the show does not reference her cameo leaving it unclear if it is still the same person.
When he entered Kamar-Taj, Strange mistakes Master Hamir for the Ancient One, only to be greeted by the real one. This is a reference to the original Ancient One appearances in the comics.
The look of the Dark Dimension is heavily inspired by Steve Ditko's design of Eternity's realm in the comics.
Kamar-Taj's wi-fi password is "Shamballa", a reference to the mystical lost kingdom and, more specifically, to the 1986 graphic novel Doctor Strange: Into Shamballa.

The surgery scene of Doctor Strange operated by Christine Palmer at the Metro-General Hospital, is nearly identical to the surgery scene of the Doctor Strange: The Oath, where Strange is operated by Linda Carter.

facts.section: Other Works that Reference Doctor Strange
facts.text: In Unbelievable Gwenpool Vol 1 #3, Doctor Strange and Gwenpool look at a theater where Doctor Strange is showing in the Multiverse. The theater had simplified versions of a couple of the posters used for the film. Doctor Strange is pleased with the choice of Benedict Cumberbatch to portray him.

Originally, Scott Derrickson intended to make Nightmare the main villain of the movie, but Kevin Feige was against it. “Kevin made a very cogent case,” said Derrickson. “The trouble with starting with Nightmare is getting across the idea of the Dream Dimension as another dimension. The movie was challenging enough. It's already an exposition-heavy movie... Dormammu made the most sense. And he is the most present villain in the comics.”

The property master Barry Gibbs revealed that the Ebony Blade was meant to appear in the movie, alongside the other relics conserved in the New York Sanctum. "That was going to go into a book called the Lexicon of Relics, but the Ebony Blade was taken out of the script. I don't quite know why. Again, as things evolved, it wasn't pertinent to the script. Things just moved on."
In an early draft of the movie, Stephen Strange was meant to become the Sorcerer Supreme by the end of the movie, but Derrickson and his crew had many many problems with that.
In concept art for the Chamber of Relics the Screaming Idol was featured.

Colin Farrell, Jake Gyllenhaal, Tom Hardy, Ethan Hawke, Jack Huston, Oscar Isaac, Jared Leto, Matthew McConaughey, Ewan McGregor, Keanu Reeves and Benedict Cumberbatch were all considered for Stephen Strange. Farrell previously portrayed Bullseye in the 20th Century Studios production Daredevil. Gyllenhaal later played Quentin Beck/Mysterio in Spider-Man: Far From Home. Hardy later played Eddie Brock/Venom in the Columbia Pictures productions Venom, Venom: Let There Be Carnage and will return for Venom: The Last Dance, he also had a cameo in Spider-Man: No Way Home due to Spider-Man and Doctor Strange breaking the multiverse. Hawke later played Arthur Harrow in Moon Knight and Isaac played Moon Knight in the same show. Leto later played Michael Morbius/Morbius in the Columbia Pictures production Morbius. McGregor later portrayed Roman Sionis/Black Mask in the DC Extended Universe production Birds Of Prey.

Benedict Cumberbatch was the first choice and was offered the lead role of Stephen Strange but initially had to decline due to his theatre commitments playing Shakespeare's Hamlet which will clash with the film's proposed shooting date. Joaquin Phoenix was the studio's second choice for lead role but Phoenix, after a few months of deliberation, eventually turned down the offer due his reluctance to do a multi-picture deal that was required by the studio if he signed on.

Co-Writer C. Robert Cargill revealed on his podcast Junkfood Cinema that he suggested cameos for Jeffrey Combs and the late Dick Miller but ultimately was unsuccessful in securing them. Combs had previously starred in the film Doctor Mordrid which started as a Doctor Strange film.

The film has been in development since 1986. Wes Craven was set to direct in 1992. Later in 2001, David S. Goyer was going to write and direct. In 2008, Guillermo del Toro was brought on as director. In 2014, Mark Andrews, Jonathan Levine, Nikolaj Arcel, Scott Derrickson and Dean Israelite were on the shortlist to direct with Derrickson being the ultimate choice.

This is the second film to feature Doctor Strange after a live-action TV movie featuring Peter Hooten in the lead role in 1978 that premiered on CBS, which was airing The Amazing Spider-Man and The Incredible Hulk TV series at the time.

This film introduces a new Marvel Studios logo, now incorporating elements from previous films into the animation. Like Thor: The Dark World, the previous film to introduce a new studio logo, it is the second film in its respective phase.

Rachel McAdams' startled reaction in the broom closet of Metro-General Hospital was genuine, since the mop handle fell completely by accident, and scared McAdams almost out of her skin. Scott Derrickson decided to keep the reaction in the film, since she never broke character.
A post-credits caption promises "Doctor Strange will return".

works.work: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness

facts.text: When the Illuminati confront Scarlet Witch, Mister Fantastic attempts to talk her down by relating to having a wife and kids of his own. In the comics, Richards marries his teammate Susan Storm/Invisible Woman and the two go on to have two children, Franklin and Valeria Richards.

This is the second Marvel Cinematic Universe film to reference Reality Numbers after Spider-Man: Far From Home, identifying the Illuminati's home reality as Earth-838. Unlike the references to Earth-616 and Earth-833 in the earlier film, Earth-838 is not a previously known Number. Earth-199999 is once again referred to in dialogue as Earth-616.

Wanda's grief over the loss of her imaginary children and the destruction of Vision draws inspiration from the storyline Avengers Disassembled. In that arc, Wanda regains suppressed memories of the children she had created during the earlier West Coast Avengers series. The return of these memories drives her insane, causing her to turn against her former teammates. In the comics, Doctor Strange ultimately defeats Wanda by placing her in a magical coma following the devastation she unleashes on the Avengers.

The scene in which the Scarlet Witch appears in the Mirror Dimension is a visual reference to Avengers #171, which Wanda becomes trapped in a room completely lined with mirrors and struggles to cast a hex, as any spell she attempts is reflected back at her.

The scene in which Wanda attacks and kills Professor X reflects elements of her original comic book history. Wanda Maximoff was initially introduced as a mutant and a member of the X-Men, as well as the daughter of Magneto. She and her brother Pietro were originally depicted as villains and members of Magneto's Brotherhood of Evil Mutants in their debut appearance in X-Men #4. These aspects of her background were later retconned in the 2015 Uncanny Avengers series.

The film's connection between the Scarlet Witch and Chthon, as well as Mount Wundagore, references the Nights of Wundagore storyline from The Avengers comics. In that arc, it is revealed that the Maximoff siblings were born at the base of Mount Wundagore, and that Wanda was infused with a portion of Chthon's power.

The Christine Palmer of Earth-838 mentions that she works for the Baxter Foundation as a Multiverse analyst. In the Ultimate universe, the Baxter Foundation was the organization that funded the Fantastic Four's fateful expedition to the N-Zone, the Ultimate version of the Negative Zone.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The film makes reference to the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home. Originally, Multiverse of Madness was to take place before No Way Home, but after the film was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, aspects of both films plot had to be rewritten for continuity purposes. The initial trailer for Multiverse of Madness was included after the credits of No Way Home; Defender Strange says the line "In the grand calculus of the Multiverse, your sacrifice is worth.." before being stabbed by the Ribboned Creature. This is the same line that 616 Doctor Strange said to Peter Parker when referring to the multiversal trespassers that had entered their universe on accident.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: While discussing their experiences with the multiverse, Stephen Strange tells America Chavez that he has some experience with it involving Spider-Man.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Wong reminds Stephen Strange that he is now the Sorcerer Supreme. This references the fact that Wong had previously informed Peter Parker of his new title in Spider-Man: No Way Home.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: During the attack on Kamar-Taj, Wanda Maximoff preys on one defender's fear in a manner similar to how she manipulated the Avengers' fears in Avengers: Age of Ultron.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: After America Chavez and Stephen Strange are flung through multiple universes, America comments on how composed Strange is, noting that most people would vomit after such an experience. Strange replies that it is not his first time, referencing the occasion in Doctor Strange when the Ancient One hurled him through various universes as a lesson about his attitude and to prove the existence of magic. He vomits immediately afterward.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: As Scarlet Witch dreams of her Earth-838 self, starting with a reprise of the opening theme from the second episode of WandaVision, during the scene where she tucks her sons into bed, some shots are actually CGI-altered takes from the "The Series Finale".

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: The Illuminati of Earth-838 make use of Ultron Sentries as staff, performing menial labor and guarding their headquarters from incoming attacks, similar to the intended use and purpose of the Iron Legion. The Sentries are also voiced by Ross Marquand, who took over the role of Ultron from James Spader in What If...?

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe

facts.section: References to 20th Century Fox's Marvel properties
facts.text: The character of Professor X makes his first on-screen appearance since the 2019 television series Legion. He is portrayed once again by Patrick Stewart, who last portrayed the character in the 2017 film Logan. This version of the character is inspired by the version of Charles Xavier seen in the 20th Century Fox films and the version of the character seen in X-Men: The Animated Series; As a reference to the Fox franchise, Xavier tells Doctor Strange "Just because someone stumbles and loses their way, doesn't mean they are lost forever." This line was previously spoken by a variant of Xavier to a younger version of himself in the 2014 film X-Men: Days of Future Past; As a reference to the animated version of the character, Xavier wears a green suit and utilizes a golden hoverchair. facts.section: References to the Evil Dead films

Before she was replaced by Michael Waldron, Jade Bartlett was initially hired to write the film.

There were widespread rumors that Tom Cruise would appear in the film as a variant of Iron Man known as Superior Iron Man from the comics. Multiverse of Madness writer Michael Waldron said that he was intrigued by the rumors and did approach Kevin Feige about including Cruise in the film, but he informed him that it was impossible due to his commitments to the next two Mission: Impossible films.

facts.section: References to the Marvel Cinematic Universe
facts.text: Echo is the first Marvel Studios project aimed at mature audiences, targeting a "TV-MA" rating as opposed to other Marvel Studios-produced television series primarily receiving TV-PG or TV-14 classification from the TV Parental Guidelines board.
Echo is the first time Maya Lopez goes by the codename Echo, despite appearing in Hawkeye.
Echo is the first TV series produced by Marvel Studios to have all its episodes released on the same day.
Alaqua Cox requested that everyone on the crew attend ASL classes a couple times a week.
Echo was the first TV series to be released under the Marvel Spotlight label.

The movie marks the MCU debuts of Thena, Ikaris, Kingo, Makkari, Phastos, Ajak, Sprite, Gilgamesh, Druig, Sersi, and Dane Whitman. It also marks the debut of the Eternals and the Deviants, and of Eros as portrayed by Harry Styles.

In the film, the Eternals' ship is called the Domo, and the name in itself is an Easter egg to comic book lore. There, Domo is the name of an Eternal who serves as an administrator on the Eternals' planet Olympia. He's an analog for the New Gods character Metron, right down to traveling in a hoverchair. Clearly, Marvel Studios has no intention of introducing Domo as a character, so they've simply applied the name to the spaceship instead. In the film, Sersi gives Dane Whitman the gift of an old ring bearing his family crest, which she claims she bought on eBay. In reality, given this is an ancient historical artifact, it's entirely possible she has had it since the Middle Ages. Although it's not clear in the Eternals movie itself, merchandise has confirmed the crest on the ring is the symbol of the Black Knight, which hails back to the days of King Arthur. The original Black Knight was created by Stan Lee and artist Joe Maneely back in 1955, in a sword-and-sorcery comic set in the days of Camelot, and he wielded the enchanted (and cursed) Ebony Blade. The mantle of the Black Knight has been passed down the generations through his bloodline - and Dane is indeed the current Black Knight in the comics; Given the Eternals landed in Mesopotamia, it's perfectly appropriate for them to settle around Babylon. The Eternals are associated with Babylon in the comics as well, with Gilgamesh ruling there for a time, and the Eternals Ajak, Zuras, Ikaris, and Thena battling Deviants over the city in Eternals: The Herod Factor #1. The Deviant leader Kro had an opportunity to kill Thena in battle but chose to spare her, which was the beginning of a longstanding (and heretical) relationship between the two; When Sersi and Ikaris arrive at Phastos' home, he introduces them as "Isaac" and "Sylvie." These are indeed aliases the two Eternals have used in the comics in order to fit in with human society, with Ikaris having also gone by a shortened version of the name as "Ike Harris" in the comics; It seems some of the Eternals actually lived around Camelot for a time, with King Arthur becoming somewhat enamored of Thena. Given she wound up in possession of Excalibur, it's reasonable to assume Thena may have been the Lady of the Lake of Arthurian legend. Interestingly, Marvel Comics has indeed recently retconned a connection between Camelot and the Eternals. According to Black Knight: Curse of the Ebony Blade #2, Camelot was "a city rich in marvels. A castle as like to have grown as been built, 'pon roots of no mortal ken. And borne on Celestial engines." The legends of King Arthur lie at the heart of many of Marvel's British characters and concepts, including Captain Britain, Black Knight, and the mystical realm of Otherworld where Arthur now resides; Fearing the world is about to come to an end, Sersi tells Dane Whitman that now is the time to reconcile with his uncle - wanting him to die at peace, with no regrets. It's quite a touching scene, giving a sense of how well Sersi truly understands human nature, but it's also a smart Easter egg in its own right. In the comics, Dane's uncle is Nathan Garrett, a criminal who used the Ebony Blade to bring disgrace to the name of the Black Knight. Dane inherited the Ebony Blade from his uncle in the comics; Eternals reveals Celestials implant a seed within a planet, which feeds off the world's life energy until the Celestial matures and emerges, shattering the planet apart. This idea is lifted from the classic Earth X miniseries by Alex Ross and Jim Kreuger, which is set in a dystopian future timeline where the heroes learn the Celestials impregnated Earth by placing their seed within it.
